utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry and Mr. Huber for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have the Defence appearances?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic. I'm representing Mr. Zejnil Delalic, together with my colleague Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Howard Morrison. I appear for Mr. Mucic together with Madam Buturovic and Mr. Greaves is consulting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Salih Karabdic, and I'm an attorney at law from Sarajevo and I'm defending Mr. Hazim Delic, together with Tom Moran, an attorney at law from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Cynthia McMurrey, and along with Nancy Boler, we represent Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We were going to start with Mr. Moran this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We will call Dr. Tomic. He should be out in the hallway. Your Honour, as we discussed yesterday, I'm sure the Court is familiar with this report. I'm going to go over a couple of areas. It will only take a few minutes, and then open him to questioning from the Court, if that's acceptable to you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Those who have got the report have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to have him here to be able to clarify things in the report, because it is a question of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I see there are some difficulties in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did not use our regular translator on this. This was a translation done in Sarajevo, and it was sent to me by e-mail. That was another reason why we wanted the doctor here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, first, with the -- well, as soon as he takes the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may take your seat, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, would you introduce yourself to the Court and tell them a little bit about your training, background and experience?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm Dr. Zvonimir Tomic. I'm a lecturer at the department for criminal law of the school of law at the University of Sarajevo. I was born in Sarajevo in 1951 where I graduated the from the school of law. In 1984, I defended a doctoral thesis at the University of Belgrade at the school of law. In 1990, I defended my thesis under the title "Security Measures in the Yugoslav Criminal Law." Is this enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Doctor, one other question, and it's a question I've never asked before in this Court, but will you tell the Judges what your ethnic background is?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, with the help of the usher, I have copies of English translations of certain portions of the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I would move to introduce those under the next number, whatever it is. I believe I've already given them to the Prosecutor. If I haven't, I'm sure they have got them other places.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 111/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I see you have your Penal Code in the original Bosnian Serbo-Croatian in front of you, and if you like you can refer to it. The Court has read your report and is familiar with it. However, it has been pointed out and we have talked about a few translation problems in it, one of the things I want to do is clear up some of those. The first thing I want to ask you, Doctor, is we've talked about and you're familiar with Judge McDonald's decision on sentencing in the Tadic case, the part about the maximum punishments and the death sentence. Doctor, you have to answer "yes" or "no" so the court reporter can take it down.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I have had an opportunity to review the Tadic case in its entirety, and I'm familiar with the sentence that was determined at the end of the proceedings. The court applied in that particular case, I don't know which methods were followed, determined a 20-year imprisonment sentence, and as far as I could see, the sentence was determined in respect of only one criminal offence. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The thing I want to point you to, and it's in paragraph 7, although you don't have a copy of it in front of you in Bosnian, is the part where Judge McDonald said that if a death sentence was authorised, the alternative punishment was 20 years. That's in paragraph 7 of her sentencing judgement. I want to draw a distinction between a court having the discretion to sentence to either death or 20 years, or whether the death sentence first had to be assessed and then it could mitigate the death sentence to 20 years. Do you understand the distinction I'm drawing, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: (Nods)

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Would you explain to the Court how that works?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav criminal legislation provided for capital punishment, prison, and a fine, a financial type of punishment. The capital punishment could not be determined for only one criminal offence. It always had to be determined together, alternatively, with the prison sentence, whose maximum was 20 years. That was according to the Yugoslav criminal law at the time. Therefore, the courts had an alternative, capital punishment or 20 years imprisonment or, an alternative, a prison sentence ranging from 5 to 15 years in prison. For offenders, it was possible to serve a 20-year prison sentence, and it was in a case of amnesty or pardon. So a 20-year prison sentence could be determined only for the most serious types of criminal offences, and that particular sentence, according to the law from 1976, was provided within the Federal Criminal Code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in respect of only eight criminal offences, whereas in the Republic Criminal Code, the Criminal Code of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it could be determined only in the respect of five criminal offences. With the presence of democratisation in the former Yugoslavia, at the end of the 1980s, there were a number of amendments done to the Criminal Code and the 20-year prison sentence was deleted in all of the relevant eight cases and later it was also deleted from the Republic Criminal Code, that is, the Criminal Code of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in respect of all five criminal offences for which it was provided. Therefore, a 20-year prison sentence could not be determined for any type of criminal offence, and the possibility was left for that type of sentence to be replaced by capital punishment. Is there anything else I can help you with?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, there is. I want to focus on the period between May -- the law that was in effect between May and December of 1992. First, in April 1992 by decree, the newly independent Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted the Federal Criminal Code; is that correct, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. On the 11th of April, 1992, in accordance with the decree law, the Federal Criminal Code was adopted, and this is the last edition of the Federal Criminal Code that was published before the war. This was adopted as the Republic Criminal Code, of course, with certain amendments. These amendments related to the social system, because the self-managing social system was no longer valid, and also in respect to certain other things having to do with the political system, the name of the country was no longer Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina but Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Statements were also made in respect of armed forces and so on. The rest of the text has, by and large, remained the same, especially in regard to punishment and sentencing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, let me focus, just for a second, on the death penalty and the 20-year alternative. As I understand it, and I want to make sure that everyone is clear on this, that a court could, if the death penalty was authorised by law, could assess the death penalty and then immediately reduce it to 20 years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The court always had the possibility to substitute the capital punishment with a 20-year prison sentence. So at the beginning, it was possible for the court to determine a 20-year sentence for all criminal offences for which capital punishment was provided for. The court always had the choice. It could either determine the capital punishment or 20-year prison sentence. That was one possibility. The other possibility was, even if it did determine capital punishment, a higher court, an appeals court could substitute that punishment with a 20-year prison sentence, but the first solution was commonly used. Capital punishment was provided for in the former Yugoslavia for a large number of cases as some kind of prevention; however, the criminal punishment in Yugoslavia was not imposed very often, and it was very rarely executed. I know only of two cases where capital punishment was determined as a sentence and was, indeed, executed. Here, I leave out certain trials that took place in 1970 and 1971, the cases having to do with some terrorist groups and counterrevolutionary activity, endangering of the country and so on. Those were exceptional circumstances and these cases are not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, if the court did not first impose the death penalty, what was the maximum punishment for any crime, if the death penalty was not actually imposed? Could the ...

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: The maximum punishment was 15 years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So long as the court did not impose the death penalty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: The maximum punishment was 15 years in prison, and the minimum punishment in prison was 15 days. That was the range of the prison sentence in the former Yugoslavia. It was not possible to impose a longer prison sentence than 15 years, except for the alternative with the capital punishment, that is, the 20-year alternative. If you want me to, I can explain this further on. According to the ideological concept of the Yugoslav criminal legislation, and under the influence of the Yugoslav criminal theory, during the past 20 years, the courts were in favour of rehabilitation of the offender, of the convict, because it was widely believed that an offender, a convict, can reform and readapt himself to the society and the family. These long-term prison sentences were avoided, and they were imposed only in respect of the most serious crimes and in exceptional circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, the sentencing practice then in the former Yugoslavia, if I understand what your last answer was, it was based on rehabilitation and not on punishment for the sake of punishment or to retribution or to make an example of someone; is that correct, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. When talking about the purpose of punishment within the Yugoslav criminal law, the dominant position was taken by the functional relation between prevention and retribution. We wanted to influence the offender and give him a chance to rehabilitate. The idea was also to influence others and to prevent commission of similar crimes again. At the legal level, capital punishment did exist for a number of criminal cases, but it had a preventative function.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, at this point, I would like to direct your attention to Article 48 of your Penal Code. Your Honour, that's on page 6 of the typed portion. Just so you know where all these translations came from, by the way, the typed portion was provided to me by from Ms. Residovic, and she had that translated, and the printed portion is out of Professor Bassiouni's book, "Law of the Tribunal."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As you know, Professor, all of the defendants here are charged in multiple counts, with different crimes in multiple counts. Under the law of the former Yugoslavia, if someone were charged with multiple counts, more than one crime in the same trial, when it came time to set punishment for those, did the court just set a punishment for each one and add them up, so you may get three years on one case, five years on another, ten years on another, and add them up, and you would come up with 18 years? Or did it have some other system for setting punishment where there is more than one crime in the same trial?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: What you have just mentioned relates to a provision which existed at the time within the Penal Code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and it was intended for a so-called concurrence. It's a legal -- theoretical, legal term. I don't know whether it is going to be translated successfully, but this relates to a number of crimes that were committed for one and the same person. The condition was that these crimes were tried at the same time. There were several possibilities for punishment in the former Yugoslavia for that type of criminal transaction. There were three models that were applied. The first one was the so-called model of absorption. The second one, the model of aspiration, and the model of cumulation. These principles were contained within Article 48. According to the system of absorption, when dealing with several criminal offences, if capital punishment was provided for one of the criminal offences encompassed by the indictment, the capital punishment would absorb all other punishment that could have been determined for that type of transaction. According to the same system, if the most severe sentence was 20 years in prison, so that type of sentence would absorb all other sentences. There could have been, for example, five various criminal acts and five sentences to be determined, and if the most severe sentence was 20 years of punishment, it would absorb all other sentences. This is in order to avoid serving long-term prison sentences, and this was in accordance with the principle of the socialist system at the time, that there was always hope and that the person could always reform and that the person could eventually return to his environment and lead a normal life. The second model that was applied at the criminal system of the former Yugoslavia was the model of aspiration. Aspirations regards, really, connecting with the idea of making the sentence harsher. For each particular offence, the court would determine a sentence, and then at the end, it would determine, it would impose only one sentence. According to the system of aspiration, if there were, for example, three criminal offences that were committed, and the three sentences, let's say three, five, and seven years in prison, according to the system of accumulation applied by certain countries, that would mean that the person would serve 27 years. According to our system, this would have been 15 years in prison. That is the maximum prison sentence that could be imposed according to the law. There could have been, for example, 20 various criminal acts, but the maximum penalty would be 15 years in prison, because that was the longest prison sentence that was provided for in our system. This method was applied for other criminal offences as well, for less severe criminal offences, for petty theft, for example, and similar types of offences. It was possible for example, for a young offender to spend three years committing such criminal offences, and he could have committed, I don't know, 100 petty thefts, so the maximum prison sentence for that type of offence would be 8 years. According to that principle, the sentence, the final sentence, had to be higher than the maximum sentence, maximum individual sentence. If, for example, the sentences were three, eight, nine, and ten years, so the maximum sentence could be ten years plus one month, up until 15 years in prison. If dealing with criminal offences for which this type of prison sentences were provided for. Therefore, the final sentence had to be one month longer than the longest sentence determined in respect of a particular offence, but it had to be lower than the sum of all these sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: We talked about, I think yesterday or the day before, about -- I used an example of a particular serial murderer from the United States, a man named Theodore Bundy. Do you remember our discussion about that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Mr. Bundy had murdered a lot of people over a period of years, throughout the United States. I asked you if the court chose not to assess a death sentence on Mr. Bundy, what would be the maximum punishment that a court could have assessed against Mr. Bundy under Yugoslav law? Do you remember that? The maximum in prison term, if the death sentence was not imposed, and what was that maximum prison term, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: According to the Yugoslav legal system, the maximum -- there could have been, for example, a hundred murders, and the capital punishment was provided for each of them. So if capital punishment was not imposed, then the punishment, an alternative, would have been a 20-year prison sentence. For a simple murder, a simple case of homicide or intentional killing as you call it here, there was a prison sentence that was provided for, and it was 15 years. That was the maximum prison sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: One last question, and I think that I'll be done and the Judges may have some questions and the Prosecutor may have some. Let me direct your attention to Article 142 of the Penal Code. Specifically, I want you to look at the first few words of it, "Whoever should in violation of international law, during war, armed conflict, or occupation," that's the portion I wish you to focus on. Did that law cover acts which would have occurred, say, during a rebellion or an internal armed conflict, or did that just apply to cases of international war? If you want to know the reason I'm asking, I'll tell you.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I would like to know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In her sentencing decision in the Tadic case, Judge McDonald said that this applies only to international armed conflict, but that by -- that she would look at it in sentencing Mr. Tadic. What I want to get at is whether, in fact, Article 142 just applies in international war or whether it would apply during an armed conflict that was not an international war?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: In the provision of Article 142, whoever is in violation of the international law during the war, armed conflict or occupation, it is -- the internal conflict is never mentioned. This could be interpreted both as either the international or internal conflict. So, I would not agree with the view that this refers only to international armed conflict. I don't think that that is a correct interpretation of this provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, because the Court is familiar with his report, and if you have any questions, I'm going to pass the witness. If the Court has some questions, I'm sure he would be happy to answer them, or if the Prosecutor has some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I just want to ask one question. What was the ordinary punishment provided under the Yugoslavian law in respect of wilful murder or wilful killing, the ordinary punishment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ordinary punishment was 5 to 15 years in prison. That would be for when you talk about wilful killing in Article 36 of the Criminal Code, it would be the -- I worked on this in 1991. With my students now, we're working on a new draft, but the minimum sentence is five years. The sentence could range from 5 to 15 years for ordinary murder. Now, for aggravated murder, which would be section 2, the minimum sentence would have been 10 years, so that would mean 10 to 15 years or death penalty. In other words, 10 to 15 years or death penalty, which could be substituted by a 20-year prison sentence, either in the first instance or at the appellate level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I don't have this section 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have it either, and we'll provide it. We'll get it to you today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Were there any guidelines provided by the law where death penalty provided that it should not be imposed in such cases?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: You mean the limits in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The two punishments, death or 20 years imprisonment, did the law provide any guidelines in cases where the death penalty should be imposed or in cases where the death penalty should not be imposed, or was it left merely to the discretion of the judge?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Death penalty is the most serious form of punishment in the Yugoslav Criminal Code, as well as any others, but it had certain limitations. One was the limitation in actually determining it. It was at both the federal level and the federal units which were six, and at one period, eight. It was at one point, part of the constitutional system. In 1974, after the new constitution was adopted, in 1976, a new Criminal Code was passed on 1 July, 1977. At that time, the federal units, which meant six republics and two autonomous provinces which made up the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, they were supposed to pass their own codes. So as of 1 July, 1977 until 1990, there were, actually, nine laws in force in Yugoslavia, one federal, six republican and two provincial. In 1990, the Republic of Serbia changed its constitution and denied the right of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You said on the 11th of April, 1992, the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted a Federal Criminal Code. We are more interested with the Federal Criminal Code than the earlier laws.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Under the Federal Criminal Code, because all these offences with which the accused are charged were committed after the 11th of April.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to find out. What was the position under the federal criminal law?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: In the federal criminal law, in the provisions of Article 37, the death penalty was regulated. In section 1, it says that the death penalty cannot be prescribed by the republican or provincial legislatures as the main punishment for the criminal act. In other words, it always had to be in the alternative with a prison sentence, either a 20-year sentence or a 15-year sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In Article 37, it talks about a serious crime. How do you distinguish it as far as murder is concerned? It is serious or not serious. Murder is murder.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: In Article 37, the death penalty -- again, let me -- this is a limitation in determining. Now, this would be part of the limitation of how it was going to be passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: The death penalty could be passed only in the most serious cases of criminal acts, which are provided for in the law, which means that the federal or republican legislator had to, that is, the people who worked on it, they had to assess through the concept of abstract social danger, whether a case merits to be considered the most serious crime. So my colleagues, experts, were the ones who worked on these laws and determined the abstract, the imagined danger to society. On the basis of that, certain criminal acts were construed and the punishments determined. I can tell you for an example, in the republican law, in section 2 for murder, death penalty or minimum sentence of 15 years. One of the examples that they give, whoever kills someone in a brutal way merits that penalty. What does it mean, "cruel and brutal way"? Let's say that a victim was tortured for an hour or a couple of hours, he was subjected to pain and suffering, or if the murder was committed, let's say that somebody wants to kill their spouse or their parents, and they may tell them that they will be giving them medicine, whereas, they would give them poison, and the victim is not aware that he or she is being killed. They are not aware of what is happening to them and are unable to defend themselves. They trusted them. So for a case like that, the republican law provides the death penalty. Your Honour, I don't know if I understood you correctly, the other provisions -- the death penalty could not be given particular categories for criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's go over this. Do you still have the death penalty as a form of punishment?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Can you specify which state do you have in mind, which country?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, in the Republic of Yugoslavia, the former -- yes, is this still a form of punishment in the former Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must admit to you that I'm not familiar with the new legislation of the current Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which concerns the two republics. I'm not abreast with the developments there. In the last eight years, I have not been in that country. I can maybe tell you about what is happening in Slovenia. The death penalty has been abolished, as well as in Croatia, and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the new law has not been adopted yet, but it envisages also abolishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: From your explanations, you have two situations where 20 years could be substituted for the death penalty. Apart from that, you have minimum sentences. No one could serve a term below 15 days and nobody could be punished for a period beyond 15 years. These are minimum sentences under the Republic of Yugoslavia codes; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Let me clarify one point here. The regular legal framework of the Yugoslav legislation regarding imprisonment ranged from 15 days to 15 years. That was the absolute -- the general minimum was 15 days, and the general maximum was 15 years. The prison sentence of 20 years was an exception, which was provided for in the law as a sentence for certain individual cases. This was both in the federal and republican legislations. But I pointed out that on 28 June, 1990, the eight instances in which the death penalty -- for which the death penalty was provided were deleted. They were subsequently deleted from the republican law as well, so that at the time when the war began, there was no provision for a 20-year sentence in any legal provision, in any of the laws in the former Yugoslavia. There was only the 20-year prison sentence as the alternative to the death penalty. The legislators also had to provide a specific legal framework for each individual crime. Let's say for a rape, the framework was 1 to 10 years, and this was the guideline for the courts. The range would have been 1 to 10 years. They couldn't have gone through that ceiling to 11 years, even though the general maximum was 15 years. That was the case then and it is so now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What I'm trying to stress is it appears that you adopt a provision of maximum sentences and minimum sentences. The sentencing principles of the Code adopt such a policy that you could not sentence for more than so many years and not less than so many years. It is only in respect of when you substitute for the death penalty in that singular case, that you reduce this 20-year period. Is that the interpretation of the policy of your Code?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. In other words, the death penalty could never be imposed as a single punishment for any criminal offence. It always had to be stated alternatively with the prison sentence. For example, such and such criminal offences will be punished with either the death penalty or a prison sentence. It meant that a court could impose a death penalty or ten years in prison, for example, or six, if it chose to do so. But if it opted for a death penalty, for that particular offender, that type of punishment could be substituted with a 20-year prison sentence. Finally, if the court chose to impose a death penalty without substituting it for a 20-year prison sentence, very often that death penalty was commuted to a 20-year prison sentence by a higher instance court. I believe I've been clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: One thing that bothers me, whereas a minimum sentence might be mandatory, you do not think a maximum sentence is mandatory. If you have to punish for 15 years, you need not, but you could not exceed that. So it's not mandatory to that extent. Or, as you've just said, if you substitute imprisonment in view of the death penalty, you need not sentence a person to 20 years. You could sentence him for less.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Let me answer the last part of your question first. The death penalty could not be substituted for a 10-year prison sentence. However, if the minimum prison sentence for a particular criminal offence was 5 years or death penalty, then the court could -- was the range of 5 to 15 years in prison, or death penalty in the alternative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is the minimum mandatory you could not go below that. That is what I'm saying. If it is a mandatory minimum sentence, it means you cannot punish for less than 5 years or you cannot punish for less than 15 days. If it is not mandatory, you have a wide scope within which you can punish. And similarly, except you said 15 years is mandatory, you cannot go beyond 15 years, then you say that you cannot punish anybody for more than 15 years. But when you say for five years, if it is that punishment, then you cannot go below that.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Maybe I was not clear enough. Under the criminal legislation in the former Yugoslavia, there was not a fixed punishment that was provided for any criminal offence. I mean, you could not simply have a 3-year prison sentence for a particular criminal offence. There was always a so-called regular criminal framework inside of which a sentence could be imposed. There were minima and there were maximums, and the general maximum was 15 years. In a specific case of murder, for example, the court had the possibility of imposing a sentence from 5 to 15 years in prison. That was the so-called regular criminal framework. You asked whether it could go below that framework. Yes. If certain legal criteria have been met, of course, the court could impose a less harsh sentence, and there were legal provisions that regulated that type of punishment. This was called mitigation of sentence, but it all went in accordance with the legal principles and legal provisions. It could also aggravate the sentence, that is, impose a more severe sentence. There are lots of various bases on which the court could go below the minimum of a prescribed sentence, and this was called mitigation of sentence. Also, there was only one basis where the court could impose a more severe sentence than the one provided for in a specific crime. This was in the case of multiple offenders, and of potential multiple delinquents. Of course, there were very strict conditions for the court to apply a more severe sentence. This was the only case, that is the case of multiple offenders. The conditions set for this type of sentence were set out in a cumulative way. Everything had to be fulfilled before a court can impose a more severe sentence. This is why it happened, actually, very rarely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We're trying to separate, perhaps, the practise of the courts, and the statutory provisions which make certain provisions for sentencing. It appears here, and I don't know about Article 39, but it talks about somebody talk not being imprisoned for not less than 15 days. Nothing stops a judge for imprisoning a person for 7 days. You don't have to make it 15 days if you do not think that is necessary to teach a person a lesson. But if it is mandatory and it has to be 15 days, you can't go below that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you might refer him to Articles 42 and 43. That talks about going below the statutory minimum, Articles 42 and 43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Doctor, excuse me, may I pose a question to you, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: In your expert opinion, is there any difference between an ordinary crime and a war crime regarding the punishment of the perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: The courts applied the law the same way, regardless of the type of crime. All the circumstances, of course, were taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: We have here chapter 16 and the different kinds of crimes, war crimes, are included. We have here some important differences. For instance, genocide war crimes against a human population, all of them receive a prison term no less than 5 years or capital punishment, only these two parameters.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: While assessing or evaluating the punishment, the court takes into account the specific criminal offence and the specific offender, perpetrator, and, of course, the legal provisions as regards punishment. In the case that you have mentioned, the punishment is the same as in the case of an aggravated murder. The court would apply the law in the same way, regardless of the nature and the type of criminal offence. You are faced with a criminal offence. You have to determine what the circumstances are. You have to pose a valid legal qualification of a particular criminal offence, and you have to take into account all relevant circumstances which might influence the type of sentence within the legal framework that is provided for that particular criminal offence. Therefore, the court has to assess the personality of the offender in its entirety and to evaluate the circumstances of the commission of the criminal offence. On the basis of that, it reaches its decision as regards the punishment. Aside from that, it could not go outside the legal framework. The specific criminal offence, the type of criminal offence, was not important in and of itself. There were, of course, pressures which could be exerted on the court, but the court always had to apply relevant, legal provisions and could not go outside the framework. Of course, there is no judge who likes to see his decisions reversed or quashed by higher instances. So they were quite careful when determining their sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: You are telling me that for this law, it's the same to be a serial killer or a war criminal, it's the same for the judge applying the law? It's the same, exactly, to punish a serial killer or a war criminal?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, it is possible for the court, for the judge or a particular Trial Chamber to have its objective approach as to whether the perpetrator was a serial killer or a war criminal, but regardless of their intimate conviction, they had to respect the parameters of the punishment that were prescribed for by the law. So regardless of their attitude, their subjective attitude, towards the offender, they had to stick to certain legal parameters. Of course, if they are not careful about how they weigh between their intimate convictions and legal parameters, they could see their decisions quashed by a higher instance. This legal framework always had to be respected, regardless, again, as I say, of the specific criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Of course the legal parameters have to be respected, but we are talking here of a prison term no less than 5 years or to capital punishment. These are the legal parameters talking about war crimes in your Penal Code; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO-BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of the Penal Code?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The entire Penal Code, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The section relating to homicides?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not have that. I've been looking for the SFRY Penal Code in English for months. As far as I know, it does not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In Article 37(2), that even in the case where the death penalty is provided, it's to be imposed only in extremely hard cases of serious crimes. The guideline is there, 37(2). Have you got a copy of the Penal Code?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: We have numerous copies in Bosnian Serbo-Croatian, but that does neither you, nor I, any good. We have been looking for the Penal Code in English, and we can have individual sections translated, but, frankly, to translate the entire Penal Code would be a Herculean task. The Prosecutor may have done it. We just don't have the resources to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: As I read this, Article 37(2), the death penalty is not to be imposed ordinarily. It is to be imposed only in the extremely hard cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, I believe. In fact, if you like, there were two cases that Dr. Tomic told me about where the death penalty was actually applied. If you'd like, he can tell you the facts of those cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Those were extremely hard cases. So that's the guideline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I concur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ordinarily, it's not the death penalty. That's why I want to have a look at the Penal Code. What are the penalties provided for?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: For homicide?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Karabdic will make a note, we'll get that translated, and we'll get that to the Court as quickly as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's a half reading, because I just got it, the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will get those provisions of the individual sections of the Penal Code. We can get those translated, and we can get them to you. If not today, we can get them to you tomorrow, because it is such a -- the task of trying to translate the entire thing is beyond our resources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What about Appendix 3 of what you just circulated here? It has Article 143, war crimes against the wounded and ill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We thank Professor Bassiouni for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, here, it's fairly clear that you could sentence someone to a prison term of not less than 5 years or to capital punishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So it's in the alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. On that, I think the Professor might want to talk about that, picking Article 143, the one you used, when it says a prison term of no less than 5 years, whether that could be a 50-year sentence or a 30-year sentence or whether it is 15 years. I think the Professor might want to speak to that. I think also, Judge Odio-Benito, that might have been your question that was not answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Professor, if I could draw your attention to Article 143, and that's the one that the Presiding Judge was just talking about. Down at the bottom, it says, "Shall be sentenced to a prison term no less than 5 years or to capital punishment." When it says "no less than 5 years," could the court assess a 75-year sentence or a 99-year sentence, or was the court limited to a 15-year sentence if it did not impose capital punishment?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: In this case, the legal framework that is provided for punishment, the minimum is 5 years, which means from 5 up to 15 years in prison or, alternatively, a death penalty. The prison term ranged from 5 to 15 years, and the 20-year prison term functioned only as a substitute for a death penalty. There could not be a prison term of, let's say, 16 or 17 years. That was the relevant legal framework, that is, the minimum was 5, the maximum was 15 years, or a death penalty in the alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How do you then explain clause 2 of Article 38? That takes the upper limit --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Which paragraph do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Clause 2 of Article 38.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: For crime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I'll read it for you. "For crimes for which the death penalty is provided," and Article 43 is one where the death penalty is provided," the court can pronounce imprisonment for a term of 20 years" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Judge, we're having a technical problem. We're not getting the English through. That's why he said he didn't have a translation. He's not getting our English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Through the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Something has happened, if we could check the interpretation. Your Honour, I see he has, apparently, done what I do every day, which is lay my hand down on the panel, and the next thing I am doing is hearing Bosnian through my earphones. I think he has done the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Professor, Judge Jan was directing your attention to Article 38, Section 2 of the Code, which says, "For crimes for which the death penalty is provided, the court can pronounce the term of imprisonment for 20 years."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Judge Jan, I think you wanted him to explain how that operated; is that correct, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is a different provision from the general, which he says you cannot imprison for more than 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's a separate situation, because under Article 143, as a minimum sentence of 5 years or capital punishment, and that is a provision for which the death penalty is provided. So you can sentence up to 20 years under Article 143, despite the general provision of Articles 37 and 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It's 38(2). I think the Professor will tell you how that worked, how that was interpreted by the Yugoslav courts, because all I have is exactly the same wording that you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let's draw his attention to clause 3, going up to 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Professor, could you take a look at Articles 38, subsections 2 and 3, and explain to the Judges how that worked, how your courts in the former Yugoslavia, the former SFRY, interpreted those provisions?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: You see under paragraph 1 of Article 38, a general law was given, and it says, "The prison term could not be shorter than 15 days and not longer than 15 years." This is the relevant legal framework for this type of criminal offence. Paragraphs 1 and 3 are some kind of -- 2 and 3, I'm sorry, are some kind of exceptions to the general law. In a possibility of prescribing a 20-year prison term was provided as an alternative for the death penalty. The criminal offence that you mentioned from Article 143, for that type of criminal offence, the court could prescribe a prison sentence ranging from 5 to 15 years. It could also impose a death penalty, and it could substitute that penalty with a 20-year prison sentence. It had to take into account the personal circumstances of the offender, the circumstances of the case, the general state of the individual, the perpetrator, such as his health state and so on, his personal circumstances and so on, whether his final punishment will be 6 years or a death penalty, that was upon the court to assess. The court, of course, had to take into account all the circumstances that I have mentioned, including the modus of the perpetrators and the consequences that resulted from his commission of the criminal act. So, it has to view all these circumstances in their entirety while assessing the appropriate type of punishment. It had, of course, to take into account the mitigation circumstances and aggravating circumstances. On the basis of the whole of these circumstances and conditions, the court was able to assess an appropriate sentence for a specific perpetrator for a specific criminal offence. As regards the provision from paragraph 3 of Article 38, this is a provision that I have already mentioned. If a criminal offence was committed with premeditation, the sentence prescribed could be up to 15 years in prison. It was also a possibility of imposing a 20-year prison term. This particular case happened some time, as I already mentioned, in 1970, 1971, and it related to a very specific case, but this is not a relevant case, because we are dealing with completely different cases here. This is a general provision which was of an instructive character as regards to federal legislation and also legislation of the republics. It was used on one particular occasion, and later on, it was established that these provisions were not really relevant and could be used only in very exceptional circumstances. They were no longer necessary as part of the Criminal Code. Later on, they were deleted. They no longer exist in our Criminal Codes. Only this general provision has been retained, which, in practical terms, does not mean a lot. Are you happy with my answer? Do you want me to explain further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You say these provisions are deleted, because here we're dealing, largely, with war crimes. Are they not part of the Penal Code?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: If you look carefully at my report, you see that I state it quite clearly, criminal offences for which that punishment was provided. I don't know about the pages. In my version, it is on page 10. It's the Bosnian version. I could, perhaps, draw your attention to the relevant parts of my report, but I need some help with the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I have in mind your argument that wanting the lesser sentence than death is by way of mitigation, but here we have a different opinion, because the death sentence is not the ordinary punishment for wilful murder. It's only in extremely serious, hard cases, and then we have this part too of Article 38 that the court can read it as a punishment, maximum punishment of 20 years. I was looking at that from that angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Your argument is that the conversion of the death penalty into 20 years or 15 years, whatever it is, is by way of mitigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's the way it was explained to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It doesn't seem to be borne out by the wording of the statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the Professor can talk to that because people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is talking about the fact that the death penalty is a very real thing, and he is talking about the events that took place in 1971 or 1979, or whenever it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Those were pretty brutal but ordinary murders, as he described them to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Extremely hard cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The way that it was explained to me, and I have been over it with several people, was the way it says in the argument, but if I'm wrong, the Professor can tell me I'm wrong and I'm willing to -- he knows more about it than I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Sometimes, the words in the statute themselves are not so ambiguous as to look for other explanations. If a war criminal is to be treated in a particular way, do you think you need somebody else to tell him how to treat him if the statute is fairly clear as to what you should do?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't know about the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you read Article 143, it's very clear. It does not say more than a war criminal who is wounded and ill, if you treat him in a particular way, it is aggravating circumstances that it appears to look like. How are we supposed to deal with the accused person in a particular way?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me see if I'm framing both of your questions right and see if I can frame a question to the Doctor that might help clear both of them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let's go to Article 143 for a second, Doctor, where it prescribes a prison term of not less than 5 years or capital punishment. Then when you go back to Article 37(2) it talks about --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: 38(2)? Okay. 38(2), it talks about the court can pronounce a term of imprisonment for 20 years for crimes for which the death penalty is provided. Now, focusing on Article 143, if a person were convicted of Article 143 and the court did not impose a death sentence under the provisions that it's an extremely hard case, what would be the punishment that the court could assess, and I'd like you to focus, in your explanation, on the interpretation of Article 38(2) by your courts. That's what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's break here. We'll come back at 12.00 so that he might have to think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll let him think about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Clauses 2 and 3 are exceptions to clause 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have found a translation that I didn't know we had of the Bosnian Penal Code regarding murder. We're waiting for the copier to warm up. It's just been handed to me, Judge, so with the usher's assistance, I believe we have sufficient copies for the Prosecutor. In fact, it appears to be an OTP document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I was going to tell Defence counsel I believe we had found at least Article 36, the homicide section of the Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That may be what we're passing out. I didn't keep a copy. If the usher would be so good as to give me a copy so that I know what we're introducing. Your Honour, I think that may answer some of your questions. Over the break, we had a discussion with the Professor, and I think there was a miscommunication on -- he didn't understand the question that was being asked or maybe I didn't phrase it as artfully as I could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Professor, could you explain to the Judges Article 38(2), how that was interpreted by the courts of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Regarding Article 38(2), which provides for an exceptional possibility of pronouncing a term of imprisonment of 20 years, this was something that the court could take into account and select between a prison sentence of 5 to 15 years in prison and the death penalty. The court could compromise a solution, so it could pronounce a sentence of that length, taking into consideration the purpose, the general and special prevention, and if it would find that the death penalty, in the context of a specific crime which had been committed, and the personal traits or characteristics of the perpetrators, and would come to a determination that the death penalty should not apply, but would also find that a 15-year prison term would not be appropriate, then this was a safety valve, of sorts, to avoid the death penalty and that the death penalty be confined to the most extreme cases, and yet the 15-year prison term would not be appropriate either. This is why there were very, very few death penalties which were pronounced in Yugoslavia, and even if they were pronounced, they were commuted to 20-year sentences. As I mentioned previously, I am aware of only two death penalties which were not commuted and for which a pardon was not granted eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, does that answer your question? Judge Jan, I think you were the one who posed that question. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As long as it's to your satisfaction, because that's why we're here on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Article 38(3) talks about a crime committed with intentional fault. The prison term of up to 15 years is provided. A 20-year imprisonment can also be pronounced in severe forms of such crime. How did the courts of Yugoslavia interpret that provision? What was the interpretation that was given to it by the courts?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I mentioned earlier that this was a provision in law that was present for both the federal and republican laws. In section 3, it says, "For the crime committed with intentional fault, the prison term of up to 15 years is provided." Let's say for a murder, for severe forms of such a crime, a 20-year prison term can also be pronounced. This means the legislature, let's say the federal legislature, for a specific case, or the republican parliament of the former Yugoslavia could also adopt such a law. When this law was changed in the mid '70s, it looked attractive because it appeared flexible with respect to certain abstract concepts of crime. However, the practice showed that this provision remained a dead letter. Even in cases for which it was pronounced, it was never applied. I can give you an example of eight criminal acts for which the 20-year prison sentence was prescribed. It would be a minimum of 5 years or a maximum of 20. So it would be 5 to 15 or 20, and 16, 17, or 18 were not an option. If you want me to, I can give you those eight -- they were very serious criminal acts. These are all qualified acts, and they were aggravated acts. This was a qualified case of disclosure of a state secret, so it would be a minimum of 5 and a maximum of 20 years in prison. Then the most serious acts of falsification of money or symbols of value, and very serious cases of plunder, issuing unpayable cheques, plunder by misuse of professional position, or plunder of weapon or parts of fighting instruments, and, finally, serious cases related to endangering air traffic. That meant kidnapping an aircraft and endangering the safety of a flight. This was something that was topical in the '70s, and there were very serious consequences of that, which is why the federal legislature provided special provisions for prison terms of up to 20 years. On June 28, 1990, new amendments were adopted, and the 20-year prison sentence with respect to these crimes was struck. Even though the general provision of the law was kept, it is only a general provision, and it allows a possibility for the legislature to prescribe, but not for a judge to apply. In other words, this provision is more of an instruction for the legislature, regardless of whether it is federal or republican, and it opens a possibility for them. But with respect to the Criminal Code of the then Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, such a sentence was only provided for five crimes, again, serious crimes against the health of people, the making of false papers of value, plunder, serious crimes against security of people and properties, and serious crimes against safety of public traffic. For instance, when there was a very serious traffic accident, and let's say the driver was taking school children on an outing. They sit down to relax. He had something to drink and then had an accident, and 12 children were killed, or something like that. However, through the amendments of the republican laws of July 1991, such crimes, that is, such a 20-year sentence was struck. Some of the acts -- the robbery was completely struck, whereas, again, those 20-year sentences were also struck, and only the general provision remained, so that this alternative disappeared, the maximum prison sentence or the 20-year sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: During the period we're focusing on, which is between May and December 1992, are you saying that there were no crimes in the former Yugoslavia, in BH, Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for which Article 38(3), the 20-year sentence, applied; is that correct, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I have a copy of both the Federal Criminal Code and the Republic Criminal Code. I can point out the specific or relevant part. You will see that there is no provision for a specific criminal offence for which a 20-year prison term is prescribed. That simply did not function in practice at the time. The only thing that remained was a 20-year prison sentence as a substitute for a death penalty. This was in accordance with the principle of the rehabilitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If the Court has no further questions, or if there's nothing else I need to clarify, I would be happy to pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We have an expert in the criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we thought about using her as the expert, but we thought that that might create a slight conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I hope that I will be of some assistance to return you a favour, because I have learned a lot from you. I hope I can teach you something from our legal system and practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for allowing me to proceed. Good morning, Dr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Edina Residovic, and I represent Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Is it true, Professor, that we have known each other for a very long time?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We need not mention the exact number of years we've known each other. Professor, I'm sure you know that the Rules of this Tribunal, that is, the provision contained within Article 101, paragraph 3, that the possibility was given to this Criminal Tribunal to have in mind, to take into account, while assessing the appropriate penalty, the usual practice of determining sentences before the courts in the former Yugoslavia. Are you familiar with this particular provision?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I will, therefore, ask you to discuss this particular issue so that we can facilitate the task of this Tribunal, that is, the determination of sentence and a possible pronouncement of sentence, if it should decide that one of the accused has, indeed, committed a criminal offence. Professor, could we kindly go back to the discussion you had with my learned colleague Mr. Tom Moran in connection with the application of Article 38 of the general part. I think we should tell this Court that there are two parts in our criminal legislation. There is the general part, which is intended for courts and the legislator, and the second part which analyses various specific criminal acts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These individual criminal acts in the former Yugoslavia, including Bosnia and Herzegovina, were divided in two parts, that is, the Federal Criminal Code and the Criminal Code of the six Republics?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To be more specific, criminal acts against international law were provided for in the Federal Criminal Code, whereas, murder, theft, and so on were provided for in the Criminal Codes of various Republics?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us repeat the provisions contained in Article 38, while bearing in mind the concrete application of these provisions before the courts in the former Yugoslavia. The courts in the former Yugoslavia, while assessing penalties, were bound by the framework that was prescribed for the relevant criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If, for a particular crime, there was a minimum sentence that was prescribed, then the maximum was 15 years in prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not necessarily so, because the general maximum was 15 years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the legislator could also impose a specific minimum and a specific maximum sentence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. For each criminal offence, there was a specific criminal framework in terms of sentencing, and the legislator would use various models while imposing these frameworks, these parameters. For example, there was a so-called closed model of a legal framework. For example, a criminal act carries a sentence from 5 to 10 years in prison. That was a specific minimum that was prescribed for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe this is quite clear for the Court. What it means is that a court could impose, could pronounce, any sentence between 5 and 10 years in prison. However, if that specific maximum was not indicated, was not prescribed, then the court could also pronounce a sentence ranging from 5 up to 15 years in prison. This maximum could never be exceeded, except for exceptional circumstances which were provided for in the law?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. If no mention was made of a specific maximum penalty, then it was thought, it was understood, that the maximum would be the general maximum provided for by our law, that is, the 15 years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Jan drew your attention to the provision contained in paragraph 2 of Article 38, which provides for the possibility of substituting the death penalty with a 20-year prison sentence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, whether this particular legal provision was, indeed, applied in practice of the Yugoslav courts, in such a way as this was a power of the court that could be used when the court believed that the 15-year prison sentence was not harsh enough and the death penalty was deemed to be too harsh. In that case, the court opted for a 20-year prison sentence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a general rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The death penalty, under Article 37 was to be imposed only in extremely hard cases. Therefore, the ordinary punishment would be in cases where the law prescribes a death penalty governed by clause 2 of Article 38. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the word "prescribe" is mentioned, it means that the law is giving the right to the legislator to determine which are these cases, which are the most serious crimes?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it is not the right of a judge to determine which crimes are the most serious crimes. A judge could not determine that a particular situation was a situation where the most serious punishment could be imposed?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. No judge could create a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judge Jan asked you something about a murder, a murder is always a murder. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true to say that, under our republic criminal legislation, a premeditated murder carried a penalty ranging from 5 to 15 years in prison, and that a judge, for a simple premeditated murder, could impose a sentence which fell under this framework, that is, 6, 10, 14, or 15 years in prison?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The maximum was 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that the legislator, and not the judge, prescribed the most severe cases of murder in which and for which an alternative for the prison sentence was also a death penalty?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was prescribed by the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You're referring to Article 36, paragraph 2 of our Criminal Code?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was only in that case, and you have mentioned only two cases of aggravated criminal offences, namely, aggravated murder, murder committed out of revenge, and so on, and only if the facts established for that particular criminal case lead the court to believe that it is this aggravated type of criminal offence that's been committed. Only once that has been established the court can then decide whether to pronounce the most severe prison sentence, that is, the 15 years in prison, or it can opt for a death penalty. Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If the court, in a specific case, decided that the prescribed sentence was not adequate for the seriousness of the case, and if it decided that it should apply the alternative, that is, the prescribed death penalty, is it true, Professor, that at that moment, in that case, the legislator, on the basis of Article 38, paragraph 2 of the Federal Criminal Code, gives him the possibility to substitute that death penalty with a 20-year prison sentence? Is that the correct interpretation and application of legal provisions in our courts?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. This would be the appropriate application of that provision.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us review a few articles which were pointed out to you by Judge Odio-Benito, namely, criminal acts provided for in the special section of the Criminal Code, that is, the criminal offences against the international humanitarian law. I believe that the Judges have the translation of Articles 142 and 143. Professor, I would kindly ask you to discuss now the application of these provisions, namely, the provisions which carry a prison sentence with an indicated 5-year minimum and the alternative penalty being a death penalty. When the courts in the former Yugoslavia were faced with such a situation, that is, with a necessity to establish that a serious criminal offence was committed, is it true that the court had an alternative of pronouncing a 5-year to 15-year prison sentence, depending on the particular circumstances of the case, of course, or its alternative, to pronounce a death penalty for that particular criminal offence; is that correct, Professor?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If our court opted for a prison sentence, it means that it could easily pronounce any sentence ranging from 5 to 15 years in prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, if the court opted for a death penalty, it had the power, it had the authority, in accordance with general provisions, to replace, to substitute the death penalty with a 20-year prison sentence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you are probably familiar with one such case which was tried before a court in Bosnia and Herzegovina and which took place in 1980 and which was finally adjudicated in 1981?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with it. I know which case you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This was the only case of a war crime that was ever tried before our national court?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was a case of a war crime committed against the civilian population in 1941, and it was an aggravated case of that crime. It was committed under exceptionally severe circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The male population of one village was killed?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Women were killed and underaged children were also killed?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in that particular case, the first instance court substituted the death penalty with a 15-year prison sentence. And in the case of one of the accused, the death penalty was substituted by a higher instance court with a 20-year prison sentence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The court dealt with an exceptionally severe case of murder, including murder of women and under-aged children?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a very severe case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yet the court in Bosnia and Herzegovina did not opt for capital punishment?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in spite of the seriousness of the case, there may be some significant mitigating circumstances which characterise not only the perpetrator but the crime itself?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When a court finds exceptionally mitigating circumstances, even in the case of such a harsh offence in respect of both the perpetrator and the circumstances of the crime, is it true, Professor, that the court in that case is not bound by the minimum prescribed by the law?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, if the circumstances are such in the application of these particular provisions before the courts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the court had the right to further commute the minimum 5-year sentence and to finally pronounce a 1-year prison sentence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, it is the mitigating circumstances that provide the court with the possibility to pronounce a sentence, even in such grave cases, ranging from 1 to 15 years in prison; was that the case?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. The situation is identical in cases of qualified murders. In the case of a qualified or aggravated murder, mitigating circumstances are also taken into account, and the sentence can be commuted to a 1-year prison sentence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The sentence can be reduced. If I can explain, we're dealing with general provisions of the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia, which related to any perpetrator and any criminal act.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Let me go back to the question asked by Judge Jan, when he asked you whether a murder is not a murder in any case. We have seen very serious cases of murder, and we call them qualified murders in accordance with our legal practice, in accordance with our law?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, there are less serious types of murders which we call privileged cases of murder?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we are familiar with the institution of unintentional murder --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Murder and homicide. All homicides are not murders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not referring to homicide or I'm not referring to unintentional killing. However, I would like the Professor to explain to us the fact that there are two other types of premeditated murder under our criminal legislation, namely, wilful murder, that is, the case where the perpetrator acted out of his emotions and could not resist committing the crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct, and there is a sentence that is prescribed for that type of murder.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Professor, that premeditation is necessary for a person to commit a murder?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, it is also possible for a perpetrator to want to intentionally wound someone, and that his intent results in death?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true then that we have, under our legal system, the institution of infliction of serious bodily harm?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And a much lesser sentence is prescribed for that type of criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. For a simple type of murder, a simple type of murder carries a 5-year to 15-year prison term. For that specific criminal act that you mentioned, infliction of serious bodily harm which results in death, is different in terms of criminal responsibility. Therefore, the criminal responsibility is assessed differently in view of the consequence that resulted from that type of criminal act, that is, the infliction of bodily harm.
