The death that resulted is not the result of his premeditation. What the result of his premeditation is the serious bodily harm, however, the death was not premeditated. So in respect of the consequence, the sentence was significantly different, that is, that in that particular case, it ranged from 1 to 10 years in prison, although in the end, because of the consequences, it looks the same, it is not the same case because of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have spent several years analysing these problems. Would you agree with me if I say that the court practice of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which, let me say, was one of the most harsh, most severe in the former Yugoslavia, always took into account the minimum of the prescribed sentence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. In most cases, the penalties that were pronounced were at the level of the specific minimum that was prescribed for a particular criminal act. Let me give you an example for that. In cases of murder, the usual sentences that were pronounced for a simple murder, the one contained in Article 36 of the Bosnian Criminal Code, the sentences ranged from 6 to 6.5, in spite of the fact that the law prescribes a maximum of 15 years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: In some other cases, the sentences were even less harsh.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. With the permission of the Court, if the Court believes that these issues have been clarified, I would like to move on to another area which might be of interest in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your report, Professor, you make mention of a special institute of our criminal practice and legislation, that is, the mandatory application of a less harsh sentence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is provided in Article 4 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY. Could you tell us what is the basic rule, which law is applied by our courts while pronouncing the sentence according to the principle nulla crimen sine lege, and when applying that principle, are there any exceptions in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I just clarify, make sure there's not an error, when you said Article 4 of the SFRY, do we have a translation of that or did you mean Article 40?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Article 4 of the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which speaks about the mandatory application of a less harsh criminal legislation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I ask if any counsel has a translation of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since it is not a very long article, I can read it out to you. It is possible that we have the translation, but I will read the text of the article, and on the basis of that, the Professor will provide his interpretation of the article.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The title of this article is "The Mandatory Application of a Less Harsh Criminal Law." Paragraph 1: "In respect of the perpetrator of a criminal offence, a Criminal Code which was valid at the relevant times shall be applied." Paragraph 2 reads as follows: "If, after the commission of the criminal act, the criminal law was amended on one or several occasions, the criminal law which is less harsh in respect of the perpetrator shall apply." Professor, would you kindly explain the meaning of this provision and tell us how it was applied in practice? I have read the relevant text. Let me ask you a specific question: Which law is applied by the court when assessing or pronouncing the sentence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: As you said, paragraph 1 of Article 4 provides for a general principle in respect of the perpetrator of the criminal act in accordance with the Yugoslav criminal law. The law that was always applied, that had to be applied, was the law that was valid, that was in force at the time of the commission of the criminal act. That was a general principle, and there was only one exception to that rule, to this basic provision of the Yugoslav criminal law, and that case is provided for in paragraph 2 of the same article, Article 4, where the federal legislator, on the basis of a constitutional provision, and it's the federal constitution that I have in mind and Article 211, paragraph 3, Article 211, paragraph 3 of the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, on the basis of that provision, the legislator had an obligation to prescribe a provision relating to the mandatory application of a less harsh law.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Will you please allow me to finish? From the time of the commission of the criminal act until a final judgement is reached, if, during that period of time, the law was amended on one or several occasions, the court was bound to apply the law which was less harsh in respect of the perpetrator. That was a constitutional obligation. If the court did not act accordingly, it would commit a serious mistake, and its verdict would eventually be quashed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I think you have answered my question. This mandatory application of a less harsh sentence was mandatory for courts?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since our Rules, the Rules of the Tribunal, provide for an obligation to take the national practice into account, I would like you to dwell on the practice of our courts, that is, the courts in the former Yugoslavia. I will ask you to comment on what I will say, to confirm it or not. Is the true, Professor, that if a new law ceased or stopped to qualify a particular act as a criminal act, then the court deemed that that particular law was a less harsh law for the perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Professor, that the courts deemed and applied, as a less harsh law, that law which provided for a less harsh sentence, a prison sentence instead of a death penalty, a fine instead of a prison sentence? Was that considered to be a less harsh law?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the law that reduced, that deleted the minimum sentence was also considered to be a less harsh law in that respect?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the courts would accept, as a less harsh law, that law which provided for the possibility of the perpetrator to be exempt from punishment?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, Professor, there were cases of a law being passed, a law that abolished a specific minimum and increased, at the same time, the specific maximum for a particular criminal offence. I would like to know how courts treated that particular law. For example, the former provision was 3 to 10 years in prison, and later on, the law established a 15-year prison sentence. Could you explain to us how that particular law was then applied by courts in terms of this lesser minimum and higher maximum sentence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: In these cases, the court practice, used as a legal framework, thought that the legal framework was unnecessarily too narrow. When a new law was passed which made it wider, that particular framework -- sorry, just let me finish. If the previous situation was such that the perpetrator would be sentenced from 1 to 10 years in prison, and the current situation provided for the possibility of sentencing the perpetrator to 10 years in prison, in that case, the law that provided for a minimum sentence was applied. Of course, it is understood that the specific maximums indicated were the same. If, however, one law provided for a higher specific minimum and a lower specific maximum, in that case, that law could not be considered to be less harsh.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think you've made a mistake, a higher specific maximum?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We are now discussing the application of a less harsh law. In any case, the lower specific minimum was considered to be the most important. At the same time, the specific maximum also had its significance. If, for example, the court should decide to apply the law carrying a lower specific minimum and a higher specific maximum, in that case, the sentence that was eventually pronounced could not exceed the specific maximum that was provided for in the law that was found to be more harsh for the perpetrator, because, in doing so, the court would have made a judicial mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before we break for lunch, I would kindly ask you to spend a little more time in explaining this. For example, if, for a specific criminal act which previously carried a minimum of 3 and a maximum of 10 years, a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 15 years is now established, the court, in practical application of that particular law, could pronounce a 1-year sentence, because it is a less harsh sentence than the 3-year sentence, according to the new law. But, however, it could not pronounce a sentence that was higher than 10 years in prison, regardless of the possibility provided for in the new law which prescribed the maximum 15 years, because this would have been a more harsh sentence. The court would have applied a more harsh law, and it would have been an inappropriate application of the relevant provisions.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We have spent some time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure it's relevant. There are many countries there is a fundamental right that you can't be given a sentence that was -- I don't think it's really important for us. In many countries, there is a fundamental right that you can't be given a harsher sentence than what was described at the time when the offence was committed, although the courts might take into account that the minimum has been done away with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the break, I'll try to stick to the relevant portions, but let me first just try to finish this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, if no death penalty is provided for a specific act, is it true that the 20-year prison sentence could not be pronounced either?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. That was --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So if, for example, life imprisonment is provided for and there is no death penalty, what would be the maximum sentence that could be pronounced to the perpetrator? Is it 15 years?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. After the break, I will discuss mitigating and aggravating circumstances in relation to the personality of the offender. However, I will try to be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we can now break and reassemble at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.03 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, you are still on your exercise. Actually, I thought it would be better if you try to lead evidence or make cross-examinations about mitigation and things like that. We are not that confused about the position in Yugoslavia. It's not as obscure as that. Fortunately, we've had an opportunity to look at the laws, and we can make our own deductions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I pointed out, I'm going to just limit myself to Rule 101 of our Rules of Procedures and Evidence is instructing us to do. During the break, I think we finally managed to get an English translation of the Bosnian Criminal Code, and I hope that by tomorrow I may be able to provide you with a copy of the full text of the law so that you may be able to use it in the future, if you so desire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That will be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, as I just pointed out to Their Honours, I would like to take you back to what Rule 101 of this Tribunal is referring to, in other words, to see what the general practice is regarding prison sentences in the courts of the former Yugoslavia and today's Bosnia-Herzegovina. Up until now, we have talked about legal provisions, about the frameworks, and the limits imposed upon the courts. Now I would like to request that you help the Tribunal understand what the practice was in our courts and what they were taking into account when passing sentences; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Along with our motions, we provided to the Tribunal, and I believe that the Prosecution did as well, we provided the translation of Articles 41 and 42, that is, the translation of articles, and I hope you can agree with me, which provide the general rules for the determination of sentence and the mitigating circumstances which would allow the sentences to be lower than provided by in the law. We are not going to dwell on the text of the law, because we are familiar with it by now. But, Professor, can you tell me, is it true that one of the circumstances which courts consider when determining a specific sentence to a specific perpetrator is the level of his criminal responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The degree of criminal responsibility is the first criteria in that article regarding the determination of individual sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Our courts judge whether he was fully responsible or partially responsible, and the criteria are set out in our law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is all within the framework of the degree of criminal responsibility. First, the degree of accountability was used, whether it was diminished responsibility or the responsibility was completely lacking.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, we will not talk about the lack of responsibility, because that is not the case that would carry any sentence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because a person with a lack of responsibility does not have any criminal responsibility. They may be liable to some medical help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Naturally where criminal liability is lacking there will be no offence committed. You don't need to ask an expert these questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said that we were not talking about it, but the Professor still provided an answer, and I had not expected him to do so. But I'm focusing on two other criteria for determining sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, is it true that if somebody's criminal responsibility is significantly lower, that the court can actually give him a lighter sentence? Let's say if the sentence was 5 years, he can be given 1 to 3 years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The sentence centres around his responsibility, the circumstances under which the offence was committed and his link with the offence committed. So why ask these general questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are the circumstances that are taken into consideration by the courts in Bosnia regarding the length of sentences, and I just wanted to mention all the circumstances, not just what is written down in the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Rule 101 also spells those things also. They are spelled out in Rule 101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In any case, you can't give a very precise definition of what is a mitigating circumstance. There are no hard and fast rules in this regard. It is for the court to determine under what circumstances the offence was committed when determining the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that everywhere in the world, the rules are the same as with us. As Judges, you must have encountered this situation a thousand times. However, our Rule says that we need to take into account the practice of the courts in the former Yugoslavia, in other words, what was taken as mitigating circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: When determining the quantum of sentence, you take the totality of the circumstances, the whole circumstances of the whole case. You can't have any definitions or hard and fast rules that this is not a mitigating circumstance under these circumstances. I don't know what the purpose is of you asking these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you want to educate the Trial Chamber as to what is happening in the former Yugoslavia, that's a good idea. Then we have some way of knowing what is happening there. I suppose that it's helpful to that extent, but it might not be necessary for our purpose now. We've seen enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It depends upon the facts of each case, what would constitute a mitigating circumstance and what would not constitute a mitigating circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not in a position to ask you questions here, but maybe with respect to the testimony of the witness I'm going to call tomorrow, I may ask him something about the cultural circumstances regarding the activities of my client. But if I do not address such issues through the witnesses, tomorrow you may tell me that this is not a significant circumstance. I thought that it would be helpful to you to see what our courts were taking into consideration. So if you do not see this as very useful, I can stop right here and now with this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You know what is better, but I was just suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, is it true that courts also considered the motivation, the motives of why a certain crime was committed?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The motive is a very important circumstance when determining sentence. It is very significant why, that is, what motivation guided the commission of a particular offence. A murder, for instance, it could have been motivated by greed, also by mercy, to spare the victim of further suffering. So the court has to take into account the circumstances, and the sentences in these two particular instances would have been enormously different.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's see, so hatred, mercy, those would all be different motives, and our courts would accept them as specific circumstances; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that further circumstances that were being considered by the courts are the circumstances under which certain offences were committed, whether this was during special conditions such as, let's say, a storm, at night, whether the victim contributed to it in any way, so on and so forth. Was that taken into consideration too?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. All these were circumstances, and they were very important. The courts took into consideration the manner in which an offence was committed, the time, the means, the circumstances, and then the relation of the perpetrator towards the victim, whether this was a small child or a person who was defenceless, whether some relation of trust was violated, let's say as between a child and an adult, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was the previous life history also taken into account, his social status, the relation through work to his co-workers, and things like that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The life history was also one of the elements which was taken into account when determining the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Social status was also considered when considering the gravity of an offence. Social status was also considered when considering --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Not so much social status, but his involvement in socially useful or desirable activities, his positive traits, so to speak, socially speaking.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I have not finished. So these circumstances could have been positive or negative. The court needed to take into account both aspects, and only in that way could it arrive at the proper sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did our courts also have an obligation to take into account the personal circumstances of the individual, his family circumstances and so on?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was also an obligation of the court. It was very important what his family situation was, whether he was the breadwinner for the family, then what the health situation was in the family, the economic situation, whether they were permanently employed or not, and the general social situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did our courts also determine, in passing a sentence, the conduct of this individual after the commission of the crime, remorse or an effort to alleviate the consequences and his general conduct before and during the legal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were also circumstances which the courts had to take into account, that is, his behaviour after the committed crime, his preparedness to plead guilty, to feel remorse, to alleviate the consequences of the committed act. A lack of remorse was considered as a very negative factor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Finally, were there also other circumstances taken into account, so his health, his industriousness, his social behaviour, were all of these things taken, generally, into account?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The court had an obligation to take everything in, all these circumstances, which would point to a particular personality of the perpetrator of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Related to this, I only have one addition question, Professor. If all these or some of these circumstances which the court had to take into consideration to give a punishment of 6, 8, 14 years, if all these circumstances were so numerous and so significant, is it true that the court here had the authority to prescribe a sentence that was lower than the sentence prescribed in the law?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The federal criminal law of Yugoslavia, in Article 42, provided this particular basis for mitigation of sentence. It existed in cases when, in a specific case, the court determined that there are particularly mitigating circumstances which pointed to the fact that even with the mitigated punishment, the right punishment can be attained. So it could give a sentence which would be lower than the one provided by law. That would mean that if the minimum sentence was 5 years, it could have been reduced to as little as 1 year. This would be still in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have finished with the issues relating to the determination of sentence in our national courts. I have only three very brief questions for you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Have you got a copy of Article 42 to which the witness is referring, that where a sentence -- provided by the law can be ordered?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have made that provision available to you, together with our submission on the sentence. So this is annexed to my brief which concerns the accused Delalic. I mean, I have not prepared this particular provision. I don't have it here, but I can surely make a copy for you during the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I look at it correctly, what Mr. Moran submitted earlier today has, on page 4, Article 42.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The limits of mitigation of sentence is in Article 43.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Professor, as I said, there are three more questions that I would like to ask you. Is it true, Professor, that before our courts, we have one unified, one integral proceedings, including the calling of evidence and also a sentencing hearing. This is all part of one and the single process?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true to say, Professor, that if the court, if the Chamber, that is, in charge of the proceedings rejects certain evidence to one of the parties to the proceedings, especially if that rejection is confirmed by a second instance court, that particular evidence would be considered inadmissible before our courts. And it cannot be used as a basis for verdict or sentence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, what would happen if such a thing should occur, if a verdict is based on a piece of evidence that was rejected or proclaimed as inadmissible, either by the first instance or the second instance court?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: That verdict would be quashed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. This includes my examination of the witness. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Please, Your Honours, I have a number of questions, but short ones on behalf of the defendant, Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Professor, can I refer you, please, to Article 36, the homicide provisions? In Article 36, it appears that we have acts of commission, that is, active acts rather than acts of omission. I appreciate I'm reading it in translation, but each of the instances set out in Article 36 appears to relate to acts of commission, that is, active acts by the accused. Is the translation accurate in that sense?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Article 36 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in paragraph 1, a so-called simple murder is provided for in the first paragraph, with a minimum sentence of 5 years. It is a very short wording. In our language, there are only four words in this particular part of the text, and they are equivalent to the English words "Whosoever deprives another of his life." The law does not state manners in which this can be committed, in which a person can be killed, although when it comes to homicide, we are, of course, talking about active acts, about commissions. There is a series of acts that can fall into that category, like opening of fire and similar acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we can read the text of Article 36, and we can see how that reads in English. I assume, for the moment, that the translation is accurate. The reason I ask the question is if we compare it to Article 38, it is plain that the law of Bosnia and Herzegovina contemplates negligible homicide, that is a culpable omission?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: It is a big difference, of course. The basic type of murder provided for in Article 36, paragraph 1, for that particular kind of murder, the sentence that is prescribed is the minimum of 5 years, and the type, the model of responsibility, is the one that requires the existence of premeditation or mens rea. In the second case, in the case of Article 38, we are dealing with a so-called negligent homicide, and according to the Yugoslav criminal legislation, criminal responsibility was provided for negligent homicide only when this was expressly stated, expressly provided for, in the relevant law. In view of the type of criminal responsibility, because there are less severe types of criminal responsibility than the premeditation, the penalty that was provided for was between 6 months and 5 years. So you can see the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. You've actually answered my next question before I asked it which is encouraging. So it would be a fair submission to say that in the case of a finding of an act of omission, the law in Bosnia, certainly according to the distinctions between Article 38 and 36, provides for less serious penalties in the cases of omission than commission; is that a fair, if simplified comment?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. The reason I raise that point is that the indictment in this case is put in the alternative. The defendants are charged with acts of -- effectively acts or omissions, so it would be within the jurisdiction of the learned Judges to convict on an act of omission, and the obvious point I'm making is that, if we take into account the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that provides a basis for a lesser sentence. I think you've already agreed with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Please, may I turn to Article 33, the purpose of punishment. Under Article 33(1), dealing with the general purpose of criminal sanctions, in translation, one says this: "Preventing a perpetrator to commit crimes and his or her re-education." Now, I hope I'm not going into too fine a detail, but it is not plain from the translation whether the word "and" is conjunctive or disjunctive. I hope I'm not making difficulties for the translator.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: In Article 33, paragraph 1, the provision that is contained therein uses a conjunctive, that is, an "e" ending. The possibility of re-education is included in this particular provision, whereas, the two other paragraphs emphasise the special type of prevention when it comes to penalties. In the Yugoslav criminal legislation, there were other measures which had that particular role, to prevent crimes. There were eight possible security measures that were provided for under the Yugoslav criminal legislation. These measures relate only to the sentence itself, and this is something that was mentioned this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you for -- I thought it was conjunctive, because I'm going to be making a submission to the learned Judges, and I didn't want to make it on a false basis. Thank you for that. Another submission which will be made on behalf of Mr. Mucic is this. Is it fair to say that from the totality of the evidence you have given, that the judges, when applying the law, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, have an extraordinarily wide discretion, even when there are statutory minima?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. This goes to the principle of the judicial individualisation of sentence, not only punishment, but other penalties as well, release on pardon, security measures, and similar types of penalties. The courts did have very wide discretionary powers with the objective of making the best possible choice when it comes to pronouncing the specific criminal penalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I hope I'm not trespassing upon the learned Judges's patience, but I think the next question I ask is going to be more of academic than practical interest, but it is this: We see provisions for imprisonment and financial penalties. Are there also within the code, provisions for, what in England would be called community penalties, such as probation or doing free work for the community?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Your question is rather topical because of the new legislation that is being introduced in the area of the former Yugoslav countries. According to some theoretical approaches and influences from the west, numerous other types of criminal sanctions have been introduced. If we look at the particular situation in this case, for this particular case, previously, only three types of penalties were provided for, death penalty, imprisonment, and a fine, a financial penalty. It is quite clear that when it comes to imprisonment, this type of penalty, the convicts were required to work, of course, within the parameters of their psychological and physical abilities, because the work also had an educational function and some type of rehabilitational function. This was supposed to prepare the convict for normal life after the prison. If he had been convicted of theft, for example, he needed to be prepared for some other type of work after serving his prison sentence. Provisions were made for such individuals to complete some kind of trade, vocation, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Under Article 142, and this is just an example, because I think the word appears in other articles, when Her Honour Judge Odio-Benito raised that Article, it struck me, again, that it may be something that requires interpretation. There is a provision of 5 years strict imprisonment as a statutory minimum. Can you assist us? Does this strict imprisonment, as one might expect, to the regime of imprisonment, or is there another interpretation?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Up until 1976, in the former Yugoslavia, there were two types of prison sentences. The first one was a simple prison sentence and a strict imprisonment. A simple prison sentence could be imposed ranging from 3 days up to 3 years. Strict imprisonment ranged from 5 years to 15 years in prison. However, after the application of the new criminal legislation in the former Yugoslavia, the 1st of July, 1977, a unification of prison sentences has been made. Since that time, we had only one type of prison sentence, from 5 to 15 years in prison. So the same regime of prison sentence applied to a convict who received a 3-year sentence and a convict who received a 15-year prison sentence. The regimes of correctional facilities were the same. After a certain number of years, they were entitled to some home leave. At the beginning, this type of leave was done within the correctional institution, and after a certain period of time, after it was established that the convict could be trusted, that after it was made sure that he would not leave the country, such a convict could be released for home leave, and he could spend some time off with his or her family, try to help the family, for example, during the summer, if they were doing some agricultural work or building a house, for example, of course, provided that he returns on time to serve the remainder of his sentence. The regime was the same. There was no difference in respect of the length of prison sentence. What is perhaps -- the regime of a prison sentence always depended on the psychological and mental state of the convict. There were convicts who could not do any kind of work within the correctional facility. However, there were convicts who were able to take care of the garden or the yard of the correctional facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. So the reality is that the word "strict" relates to the number of years, rather than the regime?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Lastly this: You've referred to correctional facilities. Can you assist us with this, please, if it's not within your knowledge, then please say so. But going back to 1992, who were officially responsible for running prisons in Bosnia-Herzegovina? I mean, for example, in England and Wales, we have a government service and some private prisons. What was the official body responsible for running prisons in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fail to see how this is relevant to the question of the appropriate sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: It goes to mitigation, and I'll explain how, because it's a perfectly valid objection, if I may say so, if I don't explain it. The explanation is going to be this: That in part of the mitigation, on the assumption that Mr. Mucic is convicted of one or more of the counts on the indictment, one of the points that will go to mitigation is that he was not a trained prison guard or prison officer. If there was, in fact, no official body, that would not be a good point to make in mitigation. If there was an official body that had oversee of the prison service, then it is a better point, which is why I make it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My objection still stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't think it makes any difference, it's still evidence in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you think it's necessary for us to take it into account, we'll do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before you need to take it into account, the witness needs to be able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I say it is still evidence in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Can you assist us, please, Dr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The serving of a sentence in the former Yugoslavia fell under the competence of three types of facilities. There were facilities of a so-called closed type, semi-closed, and an open type. There were also prisons for juvenile delinquents, but they weren't really prisons but some kind of educational facilities or homes. This all fell under the jurisdiction of the ministry of justice of a particular republic, so this was at the level of the republic. The enforcement of criminal sanctions, in general, was governed by a special law which was called the law on the enforcement of criminal sanctions and penalties relating to misdemeanours, and I hope that misdemeanour will be translated correctly. That area would cover, for example, traffic offences. The regime at these facilities varied. The most variable regime, of course, was the one that was in force in the so-called open facilities, facilities of open type. The convicts would come to work in the morning. They would have to do the work during the day, and in the afternoon, they could go home and they could sleep at home. In the morning, they would have to show up at work again. This was a so-called open type of facility. As far as semi-open facilities are concerned, the regime was somewhat more severe and less privileged. However, these convicts could also leave the facility and could also do some work outside the correctional facility. When it comes to the so-called closed correctional facilities, of a closed type, depending, of course, on the type of the criminal offence and the severity of the punishment and the character and personal traits of the convict, classification was made of convicts, and they were divided in groups according to particular requirements pertaining to that category. They did not have the same regime. There was a category of convicts who could not leave the correctional facility at all, who were not allowed to go out. Then came the category of those who were sometimes, occasionally, allowed to leave the correctional facility under the escort of prison guards, of course, to take care of any work they needed to conduct. There was the third category of convicts, those who were allowed to leave the correctional facility without the escort of prison guards. The administration of the correctional facility in question trusted these convicts, and the convicts were very seldom abused of their trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor Tomic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, if I might be allowed just a question from here, I'll be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you so wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Although I believe that my learned colleague, Madam Residovic, has touched on this briefly, I would just like to specifically ask under Article 41, when it says that the circumstances to be taken into consideration is the level of criminal responsibility, that relates to diminished mental responsibility, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It relates to mental responsibility and the culpability as well. Do you wish me to explain this any further? When the law mentions as a potential circumstance, mitigating or aggravating the level of criminal responsibility, this meant that two things basically had to be taken into account. Under the Yugoslav criminal law, criminal responsibility consisted of mental responsibility and culpability. Both these elements could vary in degrees, in levels. So, leave aside the complete lack of responsibility, which automatically excluded criminal responsibility as such, what was taken into account while assessing the criminal responsibility was the following: The full mental responsibility, a significantly diminished mental responsibility, and one more category, which is not a legal category, properly speaking, but it has developed through the practice, and this is the case of diminished mental responsibility. So there is a very important difference between diminished mental responsibility and seriously diminished mental responsibility. The seriously diminished mental responsibility represented a special type of legal basis for mitigation of sentence, whereas a simple diminished mental responsibility could be taken into account as a mitigating circumstance while assessing the appropriate sentence, again, within the parameters of the prescribed penalty. In the first case, the courts would go under, below, the parameters of the punishment that was provided for that particular offence. In the second case, the court would remain within the parameters, legally-established parameters, for that particular punishment, but there was a possibility to apply a less harsh sentence, again, within the frameworks of punishment, for that particular type of criminal offence. Have I properly understood your question? Second, there is the show of culpability. Under the Yugoslav criminal law, the culpability consisted of two or, rather, four elements. The first type of culpability was a so-called premeditation, which could be direct or indirect. The second type of culpability was negligence which could be conscious or unconscious. Do you wish me to state legal qualifications of both? I believe that what is important is the fact that they both include intellectual and volitional elements. They take into account both the will of the perpetrator and the intellectual faculties of the perpetrator. Let me give you an example. If you have a perpetrator who, at the time of the commission of the criminal offence, was in full possession of his mental capacities, and if he committed a crime with direct premeditation, the low level of this type of -- there would be a high level of culpability, whereas, a low level of culpability would be for someone who was not fully aware and committed the crime out of negligence. So that would call for a lower level of criminal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Tomic. When we talk about those two different levels of diminished mental responsibility, one you stated was essentially diminished mental responsibility which would normally take the sentence underneath the statutory minimum, and the second was diminished mental responsibility that would not take it below the minimum, but would place the punishment somewhere close to the minimum; would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can point to the relevant provision. This is Article 12, paragraph 2, which states expressly that the perpetrator can be imposed a less harsh sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one more question about diminished mental responsibility. In the courts in the former Yugoslavia, what type of evidence was necessary to persuade the court that there existed diminished mental responsibility of the individual?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Before the courts of the former Yugoslavia, the issue of mental responsibility was not raised on a regular basis. It was raised only in exceptional circumstances when the circumstances of the case were such as to indicate the perpetrator who was not in full possession of his mental capacity at the time of the fact. In other words, when there were reasonable grounds to suspect the mental responsibility of the perpetrator, in that case, the court would request an expert psychiatric analysis of the perpetrator, and the expert in question would provide his expert opinion, which would usually take a two-month or three-month period of examination, and he would submit his written report to the court, and he would appear before the judges to explain the psychological state of the perpetrator of the time of the commission of the fact. So when it comes to assessing the mental responsibility, the court would always have a recourse to the assistance of a court-sworn expert in the area. I hope this is the case in your country as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, it is, in different levels of mental responsibility, though. I also would like to ask one more question: As far as the circumstances of mitigating evidence, a young age, age is a consideration of the total circumstances of the individual to be considered as mitigation of punishment, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The age could be taken into account while assessing the appropriate sentence. Let me give you an example. If the perpetrator was an elderly person or a person in a poor state of health, and if he was forced to steal because of his personal circumstances, the court would definitely take into account his age and his personal circumstances while assessing the appropriate sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: That also relates to fraud, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And also the young age. If someone was 18 or 19 years old, that would be considered as mitigating circumstances also, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. One can say that it could be taken as a mitigating circumstance, although for the most severe types of penalties, there were certain limitations. Although the person in question may have been of age, very often the court had to deal with the person who did not have a very rich life experience. So this type of these personality traits, relating to the age, were, of course, taken into account by our courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Tomic, since the courts in the former Yugoslavia seem to take in the total circumstances, as Judge Jan has cited, for mitigation of punishment, the court would have considered circumstances of a war and the circumstances all around the events that occurred, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: The courts were bound to take into account all these circumstances by law, and only in assessing the circumstances in their entirety could the court reach an appropriate verdict. Should the verdict be reached on the basis of only one circumstance, then the second instance court would, in most of the cases, quash the verdict in question. The circumstances, therefore, had to be taken into account in their entirety, and only that could properly function as a legal basis for assessing the appropriate sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Tomic. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any questions by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Goreta. Excuse me. Good afternoon, Dr. Tomic. Sir, with respect to diminished responsibility, you indicated that it was an exceptional defence, so you would be surprised if a forensic expert looked at 25 cases of war crimes and found diminished mental responsibility in all 25, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. Ms. McHenry is misleading this witness. First of all, the expert she's talking about took into account 120 cases, 25 of which he wrote about. I believe she's misleading him as far as the facts of the case are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can you put your question to him again?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, and I don't believe it's misleading if you look at the Article, although he later on looked at others, he said that these were 25 that he looked at. In all 25, he found diminished mental responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, my question again is, you would be surprised if a forensic expert looked at 25 cases of war crimes and found diminished mental responsibility in all 25, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can surprise him with so many things. I don't think it's a fair question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he doesn't think he can answer it, obviously he can tell me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: These are all opinions. If he believes that they can be --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: There are no problems. I can answer this question. I wouldn't be surprised at all if he determined diminished responsibility with all 25 cases. It could be that all cases that the Doctor was studying, that in all 25 cases, there was heavy intoxication, for instance. Thousands and thousands of people were getting drunk, and in this state, they committed crimes. So why not the 25 that he mentions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object, because for clarity, if he's going to form an opinion on the basis of the question Ms. McHenry has asked, he needs to know that it was a hospital where only the most severe cases were referred. So he needs to know that those were exceptional cases that were referred to that hospital ahead of time, not just 25 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you prefer being the expert in this case. Let him give his answers. That has nothing to do with your own opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You indicated that in the former Yugoslavia, judges were entitled to consider a broad range of factors, including an accused general conduct before and during the proceedings. In the former Yugoslavia, would efforts to obstruct justice be considered among the totality of the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Under any circumstance, as an aggravating circumstance, not in the mitigation of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Under the totality of circumstances which can include both aggravating and mitigating. Certainly, I would believe it would be aggravating circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, would that be something that could be considered?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I think that the witness did respond that it was a circumstance that would be considered by the courts, so I don't know why he should repeat it himself.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I do not know what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why wouldn't you allow somebody to put him questions? I don't see how it concerns you. If someone is asking questions, let the questions be put and let us have the answers. They are not answers which belong to you. Please, put your question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that efforts to obstruct justice can be considered by a judge in determining the totality of circumstances in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it could be considered when determining the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you would agree with me that, although it may change in the future, in 1992 and up to the present time, the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina does provide for a death penalty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I believe at this point the death penalty is still in force, in other words, the law that provides for the death penalty. The new law has been written, but it has not been adopted yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you were asked by Mrs. Residovic right before, I believe, the lunch break, a question about the maximum term of imprisonment for cases where life imprisonment was provided. Now, I'm a little confused, because I'm correct, aren't I, that in the former Yugoslavia, there were no crimes for which a life sentence was provided; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Such punishment was not provided for in the legislation of the former Yugoslavia. There was death penalty. It was the prison sentence of 15 days to 15 years, and then there was also the financial punishment, and then there was a confiscation of property, which was a relic from the past which was abolished. So, no, there was no life sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, the Tadic judgement, when speaking of the law in the former Yugoslavia, including Bosnia-Herzegovina, said: "Imprisonment as a form of punishment was limited to a term of 15 years or, in cases for which the death penalty was prescribed as an alternative to imprisonment, to a term of 20 years." That's a correct statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: With respect to offences for which the death penalty and prison sentence were provided, when the death penalty was not provided as the only punishment, the courts had two alternatives from the start. It could determine either a prison sentence which would be either the 5 to 15 years prison term or a death penalty, then 10 years or death penalty, which would mean 10 to 15 years or death penalty. The court had to choose with respect to the specific threat for society and the specific perpetrator whether a prison term, with the limit of 15 years was sufficient, or whether it was going to consider the death penalty. And if they -- I'm sorry. I did not finish. If they chose the second alternative, in other words, the death penalty, they still had two possibilities, to either give the death penalty or the prison sentence of 20 years, even though this 20-year term was not provided for in the law but, rather, in the federal legislation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When the proposition was put, either you reject it as inaccurate and formulate your own or you now proceed to say what you think the proposition is. The question which counsel put was a straightforward, simple one, asking whether that proposition was right. If it is right, you accept it. If it is not right, you will now tell the Trial Chamber what your own proposition is, with respect to those provisions of your ... because when you go on and on, everybody gets lost in the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was my statement correct? If you need me to repeat it, tell me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think the law is very clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that's the case, then I think this expert can easily say, "Yes, you are correct."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was this statement correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, but I answered very accurately. If there was a 5-year term or a death penalty was provided for and if it was --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Please, I don't want you to explain again. Are you able to tell me with a "yes" or "no" whether or not this is a correct statement. If you need me to repeat it, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Imprisonment as a form of punishment was limited to a term of 15 years or, in cases for which the death penalty was prescribed as an alternative to imprisonment, to a term of 20 years.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you mention the law concerning infliction of bodily harm, and I'm not going to ask you to explain anything about it, and we may, hopefully, get the copy tomorrow. But can you just tell me where are those provisions in the law? Can you just cite me to an article? I'm not asking you to explain them.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: You mean serious bodily injures.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: They were in the republican law.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: In the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina can you just, please, tell me the provision?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Article 42 of the republican law. It refers to the serious bodily injury. It is Article 42 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, during your testimony, there was some discussion that the death penalty was to be given only in cases of serious or hard cases, although everyone recognises that every case has to be evaluated individually, it is the case that the legislature of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Article 36, set out what it considered to be serious or aggravating or grave cases of homicide; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The words are extremely hard cases, not only hard cases, but extremely hard cases, Article 27(2).

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: May I begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Death penalty shall be pronounced only for extremely hard cases, not only hard cases, but extremely hard cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: With your permission, please. In Article 37 of the Federal Criminal Code which regulates issues on death penalty, in paragraph 2, it states: "Death penalty shall be pronounced only for the extremely hard cases of serious crimes for which it is prescribed according to law." So the exception is the most serious of the serious crimes for which it was prescribed. These always needed to be exceptionally serious cases. In the republican law, in Article 36, several possibilities are quoted, and I mentioned several today. I don't think there is a need to repeat them now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, I wasn't suggesting that the death penalty would be applied in every single of those cases, but I'm suggesting that the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina indicated that it viewed as serious or aggravating cases of homicide, those where someone has acted in a cruel manner, or in a wantonly aggressive manner, or out of merciless revenge, or other low motives, or where someone is guarding a person deprived of their freedom, or where two or more homicides have been committed. Is that correct, that these were viewed as serious or aggravating cases of homicide?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: In Article 36, paragraph 2, there are several alternatives offered. These are all qualified or aggravating forms of murder, and for them, the mandatory punishment is different.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: For those cases, there is a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you talked about one war crime case in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm correct that when the SFRY existed, war crimes were usually prosecuted in federal courts, rather than the republic courts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but that is not correct. Your information is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, again going to how a judge should determine what penalty should be applied, we've been given the translation of the SFRY code, Articles 41, 42, 43, 44, 45, 46, 48, 49, and 50. Do you know why we haven't been given translations of Article 47?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Am I correct, sir, that Article --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I could say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Is everything all right now? This is a provision on a particularly serious case which was deleted from the law on the 28th of June, 1990. I don't know if this is a provision which was called in the Yugoslav legal practice, a particularly serious case. Just as the 20-year term was done away with, so was this particular provision done away with. I could explain to you in an example what such a case was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No. Just let me clarify. It's your testimony, sir, that Article 47 was repealed in 1990. Do I understand you correctly? So after 1990, Article 47 no longer existed?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. As of 28 June, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I can show you the text of the law of 1990, and it says Article 47, a particularly serious case, and it says "deleted." It means that this has been done away with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What is this article about?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The article is about especially, serious cases and what should happen. If the Professor has told me that it has been repealed, I don't have any further questions. My question was, "Why wasn't that included"?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, one reason, among others, that a Chamber before this Tribunal, in the first Erdemovic judgement, found that the practice in the former Yugoslavia regarding sentences was instructive and could serve as a guide but was not binding on this Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me object to this. The Appeals Chamber vacated that judgement. That judgement is just ink on paper. It has no binding authority on anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: She is merely just seeking his opinion. I see nothing wrong with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let me continue. One reason, among others, that a Chamber found that the practice of former Yugoslavia regarding sentences was instructive and could serve as a guide but was not binding was the practical and legal difficulties in establishing just what the practice in former Yugoslavia was. I'd like to ask you a few questions about the basis for your opinions. Let me ask you specifically, are there books published with the judicial decisions in them such that one can know the facts of the case and the sentence that has all the judicial decisions in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, as in other countries, there was a tradition to have the legal proceedings published, and at the federal level, there was a monthly publication which was the court practice of the highest court, the federal and republican courts. This was very important because the court practice also helped create laws. It pointed to the good sides and bad sides. So, yes, these things did exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: They exist for both the federal and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the level of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were bulletins, and they were issued on a regular basis, and whatever was interesting in terms of practice would appear in these bulletins. So the legal experts were able to follow it and then make the necessary adjustments and corrections. So, this led to a better implementation of these laws.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Then let me then go forward and ask you, and this is just an example, since this Tribunal doesn't have the death penalty, in any event. If other experts have written that the death penalty was imposed 17 times in the SFRY, in the period 1982 to 1990, for crimes of murder, robbery leading to a loss of life and war crimes, would you be able to disagree or agree with that statement or you can't say?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I did not understand you. Did you say that this sentence was pronounced or that it was executed, the number of examples you just quoted?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir. The word was "imposed," and I can't tell you whether or not that means executed or pronounced. I can only tell you what another expert said, and my question is, would you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that question because --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I do not know where the information --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: He doesn't know what it means. How can he agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it might be fair to point out the particular expert who said so and where it was so said, and let him deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, the experts were Ivan Jankovic and Vladan Vasilijevic, and to answer the question, you can say that if it's pronounced, I would agree with it, if it means, actually, implemented, I would disagree with it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I would not agree with either, even though I know Mr. Vladan Vasilijevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My pronunciation is often a problem. If one expert says the death penalty was pronounced 17 times and another expert says it wasn't, could one go back to the monthly bulletins and figure this out, or one wouldn't know because the bulletins have certain cases and not others?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I know the death penalty was imposed very rarely and was implemented extremely rarely. I don't know where Mr. Vasilijevic found this information of 17 instances. I'm not sure about that. I know, specifically, that it was imposed and it was implemented in two cases in Bosnia-Herzegovina some 20 years ago, that it was both pronounced and carried out. It was in a case of a murder of a 12-year-old child, and it was a case of merciless revenge case, something you mentioned in reference to Article 36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you have the published work on which this statement was taken, you should mention it to him so that he will complete his researches.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can find that, but as I understood the witness, he is not in a position to say either yes or no. He says, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Because you have not been quite forthcoming of the details as to how you came to your information, because you should tell him exactly what your information was. Because if you say a general article, then mention the article.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This was over a period of 10 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The report said, Your Honour. I'm not vouching for its accuracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In most of the cases, it was just not imposed. 17 cases in 8 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe it supports his statement that it was merely imposed. Can you plead that only 17 murders in 8 years --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The expert report doesn't suggest that there were only 17 murders in Bosnia or the SFRY. It suggests that the death penalty was imposed 17 times, and I'm not vouching for its accuracy, especially since this Tribunal doesn't even have a death penalty. I'm just trying to figure out how it is that one determines what the sentencing practices were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said it was rarely imposed, and he remembers one or two cases. I'm just wondering 17 in 8 years, less than half every year, which is rare, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It's certainly not common, Your Honour. I don't disagree with that. It's an article entitled, "Sentencing Policies and Practices in the former Yugoslavia, 1994."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me go forward, sir. You would also -- I assume you would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will rise and come back at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There's a slight technical thing. The professor has to run an errand having to do with the cashier's office between 4.00 and 4.30, and sometimes they open a little late, so he may be a couple of minutes late in getting back. Just so the Court knows that it is a thing the Victims and Witnesses set up for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will oblige him. We will come back at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that in March of 1993, a Mr. Damjanovic was sentenced to death, although it was not carried out --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That's irrelevant. It's beyond the time frame that is relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't know what harm you suffer from with this irrelevancy. It doesn't affect you, even if it was answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me continue my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, it's correct, isn't it, that in March 1993, a Mr. Damjanovic was sentenced to death for seven murders and two rapes he had committed previously, although the sentence wasn't carried out?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I was present at the trial in Sarajevo. I did not follow it to the end, and I don't know whether it is correct that there were seven murders exactly. I couldn't confirm that. In any case, it was a case of multiple murder and rapes. Damjanovic was not acting alone. It was a group of people including Damjanovic and a woman who was his accessory. I do not remember technical details of the trial, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It is true that he was sentenced to death, although the sentence has not been carried out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I believe that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it your testimony that --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: If I may, if you will allow me to add something, I think that that penalty, that sentence, was substituted for a 20-year prison sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, is it your testimony that under Article 38(2), for cases where a person could get the death penalty, a judge cannot just pronounce a 20-year sentence, that the judge has to pronounce a death sentence and then commute it to 20 years; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: For criminal acts carrying the death penalty, the court could also pronounce a 20-year sentence. This is the relevant text. Therefore, it cannot pronounce it as a substitute. It can also pronounce it as a sentence, that is, the 20-year prison sentence. I think the text is quite clear and precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The judge doesn't have to first pronounce a death sentence; correct? The judge can just pronounce a 20-year sentence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes. This follows from the relevant provision.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, going to 38(3), is it your testimony that that section has been repealed?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I don't think you have understood me correctly. I said that this provision has remained, and it was in force during the relevant times of this case. However, the same provision was also contained in the law of 1976, and the explanation is the following: The federal legislator left in this provision, which is of a general character, a possibility for incorporating in the separate sections of the relevant law or republic laws for the punishment of a 20-year prison sentence to be also contained. So this possibility, this provision, from '76 was used. Later on, that particular provision applied for eight particular crimes at the level of the federation and at the level of the republics. However, on the 28th of June, 1990, within the amendments of the last reform of the criminal legislation of the country that no longer exists, this 20-year prison sentence was deleted. So there is not a single criminal offence, criminal act, which carries, expressly, the 20-year prison sentence. This is something that you will not find anywhere in the relevant and currently valid legal texts. The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in July 1991, made a reform or, rather, introduced a novelty in its Criminal Code. It followed the principle of the federal legislator, and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina also deleted provisions which were connected with a particularly serious crime, a particularly aggravated criminal offence. Therefore, in these two texts that were valid in the relevant times, there are no 20-year prison sentences provided. This text covers more than 250 types of criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do I understand you to say, sir, that 38(3) doesn't, in fact, mean what its plain language says it means, which is that a 20-year sentence can be pronounced for severe forms of crimes where there is intentional fault allowing a prison term of up to 15 years?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. The translation may be misleading. The translation that I received, the translation of this article, was that it can be pronounced. However, the text of the law is the following: For the severe forms of such a crime, a sentence can be prescribed, and a sentence can be prescribed only by a legislative body. So if there has been a mistake in translation, then no wonder we cannot understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance, Ms. Residovic. I believe that does clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Could I kindly ask the interpreter to speak up a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, if I understood you correctly, you said before, during your direct examination, that in the former Yugoslavia, one of the goals of sentencing did not include making an example of someone. Did you mean to say that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand your question. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: At least as it was interpreted to me, you were asked a question by Mr. Moran which said that in the SFRY, the former Yugoslavia, that sentences were not intended to make an example of someone?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: The question obviously relates to the purpose of punishment, to the objective of punishment. The interpretation I received was the intention, the intent of punishment.
