I presume that what you have in mind is the objective, that is, what is to be achieved with criminal sanctions, criminal penalties, to a criminally responsible perpetrator of a criminal act. Let me repeat the relevant provision, that is, the provision of Article 5 of the former federal criminal law, that is, the Yugoslav federal criminal law, paragraph 2, and I kindly ask the interpreters to be as precise as possible. Paragraph 2 reads as follows: "The general purpose of prescribing and pronouncing criminal sanctions is the prevention of socially endangering activities," that is, activities or actions which represent a danger to society, "and which violate or bring into jeopardy values of the society." So this is the general goal, general objective, of pronouncing criminal sanctions in general. However, the legislator has also stated the specific purposes of specific punishments, and I gave an example for Article 33 of the former federal criminal law. This provision is of an instructive nature and it states within the general objective of criminal punishment, the legislator states the following: "1) To prevent the perpetrator from committing a crime again and his moral re-education." This first point would fall under the category of prevention. Second is the educational role, that is, the model to be served on others. Number 3 is to strengthen morale, and you can see that this is something that is rather ideological or characteristic of the former system. This would fall into the category of general objectives, general prevention. I have also mentioned the concept of retribution which was not incorporated as such. Of course, objections can be raised to this attitude of mine. If you saw the number of criminal offences which carried that penalty, you could justifiably claim that I am wrong, but it is true that, in practice, that penalty was rarely pronounced and even more rarely imposed. As I said, I know only of one or maybe two cases having to do with a father who came from Germany from where he worked and killed his wife and six children, but that death penalty was not imposed because he hung himself while in detention. That death penalty was executed, as far as I know, in two cases only. It was executed in the case of one man and one woman who committed a merciless revenge murder. This is a so-called qualified type of murder which carries a death penalty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It's the case that sentences of 20 years were imposed more frequently than the death penalty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: You cannot say that, because the 20-year prison term in respect of criminal acts for which it was prescribed at the level of the republic was never actually pronounced. That's why it was abolished because it was seen as redundant. That's why, after 1976, it was abolished. This particular type of sentence, the 20-year prison sentence, functioned only as a substitute for the death penalty, and it was a rare occurrence, because death penalties were not very often pronounced.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. Is it your testimony that, as far as you can remember, there has not been more than one or two cases of 20-year sentences in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has been saying that. He has been saying that. He repeated that at least three times.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. There has been a mistake either in the transcript or I may have misheard. The witness spoke about two cases of the execution of the death penalties, and here I see two cases of 20-year prison sentences. These are two different things. I don't know whether this is a mistake in the transcript or whether the witness misspoke.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: I thought that you were referring to the death penalty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm just asking, in general, that although you stated there were very few cases, you only remember one or two where the death penalty was imposed, that sentences of 20 years were imposed more frequently than one or two times?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Again, it could be pronounced as a substitute for the death penalty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes. I think you've already indicated this, that, in fact, the 20-year sentence was imposed more frequently than was the death penalty. The death penalty happened rarely, and 20-year sentences happened more frequently than the death penalty; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The court could pronounce a 20-year sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have one question in re-examination, and I think I have gone way over my 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Professor, I'm a little confused, and maybe you can help me. On the 20-year sentence as an alternative to the death penalty, could a court just impose a 20-year sentence, or did the court first have to determine that the death penalty was appropriate under the law, and then it could mitigate or reduce the death penalty to a 20-year sentence? Which is it, Professor?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe it's been asked and answered. I'd object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What are you objecting for? Can you kindly explain what the position is now? I heard you said, perhaps, the 20-year term is no longer irrelevant. As far as the Penal Code is concerned, that has even been abolished. I don't know what your answer will be to all these questions. Is it true that you no longer have a 20-year term sentence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR TOMIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no criminal act, both in terms of federal and republic criminal laws, that explicitly carries a 20-year prison sentence. Such a sentence is not prescribed. What remains is the provision contained in Article 38, paragraphs 2 and 3. In relation to paragraph 2, it concerns criminal acts which carry a death penalty. In these cases, the court may also pronounce a 20-year prison sentence. It is a provision of a general character. Then we have paragraph 3 and the provision contained therein, which says that the legislator can prescribe a 20-year prison sentence for serious forms of particular criminal offences, but this is all we have at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If that satisfies Mr. Moran, then I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that satisfies me. I want to thank the Professor for coming. I want to thank you for allowing me to ask that re-examination question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor Tomic. I think this is all that we have for you. I think we're very grateful for you spending the whole day with us here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, too. I hope I've been of some assistance. I hope that my testimony will help you in reaching the right decision. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, do you have any other witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There are two other matters. One is, as we told the Court, we will be presenting a written statement from Mrs. Delic, as soon as we get it typed and presented, and we could do that tomorrow or before the end of the week, at least. The other thing is Mr. Delic wishes to exercise his right of allocution and make a statement directly to the Tribunal in mitigation of punishment. Do you care to do that now or later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If he cares to, he can be sworn and he can make his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I understand it, in the Tadic case, it was just a statement and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If he wants to make a statement, that's fine. I think that is his right to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Technically, would you like him to do it from the witness box or would you like him to do it from where he's at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: From where he sits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't understand this procedure. Is he going to be sworn and are we going to cross-examine him or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Every accused can make a statement in mitigation of his sentence. I think that's the practice in England too and in Australia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No. You're talking about the ancient dock statement, and the statement before the courts has been abolished in those jurisdictions. I don't know whether it's been abolished in England, but it's certainly been abolished in most jurisdictions. It comes from the time when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He doesn't have to be under oath. If he wants to say something in support of his case in mitigation of sentence, he can do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is he going to be subjected to cross-examination? That's my main concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He doesn't have to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to help Mr. Niemann, I don't know about the law in Australia, but the law in the United States Federal Court is pretty clear, that if a sentencing judge does not specifically address the defendant individually and ask him if there is a statement he'd wish to make in mitigation, that sentence is vacated automatically without a showing of harm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And he doesn't have to be under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No. The judge just says, "Do you have anything to say, Mr. Jones." Actually, the case in the Supreme Court Green versus United States. If you'd like, tomorrow, I can bring a copy of it. I understand that in the Tadic case, although Mr. Niemann was there and I wasn't, Judge McDonald talked about Mr. Tadic making a statement. It appears to me that that procedure has been adopted by this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic gave evidence, Your Honour. He gave evidence and we cross-examined him. So I don't know what Mr. Moran is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He took an oath?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, and we cross-examined him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I know you're relying on Rule 85 as to the accused appearing as a witness

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. He's entitled to appear as a witness and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure you can call him a witness. He's making a statement in his defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The accused can always give evidence before the proceedings. An unsworn statement, which goes back to the beginning of prehistory, Your Honours, which, in most jurisdictions, has been abolished, but apparently not in the United States, is something which is no longer considered necessary. There is a great deal of historical justification for it in its time, but it has no application in the modern court environment. In most jurisdictions it's been abolished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Here he wishes to give evidence in mitigation, not with respect to guilt or innocence, which is a fairly different thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what stage it's done at in the United States, but I'd be very surprised if it was done in the course of a trial and before the jury has returned its verdict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, in the United States, the procedure is first we get a verdict, and then we talk about punishment, if it gets to that, but the procedure that's been adopted by the Tribunal is to combine the two procedures. If the defendant is to have any way of making a statement, sworn or unsworn, to the Court in mitigation of punishment, then it has to be done at this point. I think that that is an ancient right. It's a right that I'm familiar with, and I think that most lawyers are familiar with and it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What is the position in the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: If I may assist, I do sit as a judge in the United Kingdom in the criminal courts on a part-time basis as a recorder of the Crown Court. Mr. Niemann is perfectly correct that the unsworn statement from the dock has been abolished, so far as giving evidence in the proceedings is concerned when it comes to triable issues before a jury. But, of course, it is still available for any defendant to make an unsworn statement from the dock or any other part of the court if it goes purely to mitigation. Of course, as I understand it, the course that Mr. Moran wishes to adopt is the latter, to make an unsworn statement that goes purely to mitigation. It's no more or less than if the judge asks the defendant if he has anything to say before sentence. Although we haven't had verdicts yet, of course, this is because we are having a combined hearing. If this was a procedure adopted in the United Kingdom, I am certain that he would be able, at this stage, to make an unsworn statement that related purely to matters of mitigation. I would have to say, and I apologise if this is trespassing, in any way, upon Your Honours' discretion or jurisdiction, that it's something I do constantly in cases where the defendant doesn't give evidence. I always ask him if he wishes to make a statement, if there is a conviction, and before I sentence him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't think the Trial Chamber has any apologies to make in respect of this, in spite of the fact that we are adopting a new procedure. We're convinced that, juridically, there is nothing stopping an accused person from making a statement in mitigation, if that is all he's doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, that is the law as it stands in the United Kingdom, but, of course, Mr. Niemann is perfectly correct to say that unsworn statements from the dock as to matters of evidence going to issues of guilt have, of course, been abolished, but that's an entirely separate procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: When he makes an unsworn statement, he is not cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Not at all. There is no basis for cross-examining. The only time that cross-examination comes into the sentencing procedure in the United Kingdom is if the Defence calls evidence, and that is sworn evidence. The defendant himself can make an unsworn statement, but if he elects to call evidence in mitigation, then that is usually a sworn statement, or if it isn't sworn, at least it's a statement made under a solemn declaration, but it is subject to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: You're very welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: -- we have one procedure in American criminal jurisprudence that I know of where a person is allowed to make, I presume it's called, a statement from the dock where he's talking, unsworn, about guilt and innocence. That is in trials by Court Marshall under the Uniform Code of Military Justice. This is a very different thing from making a statement in mitigation of punishment. The rule that I am familiar with, at least in trials where the court is doing the sentencing, is that the defendant, prior to the imposition of sentence, can say anything he wants to the court that he thinks may convince the court to mitigate the punishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, I did not think the accused should come into the witness stand, because he is not speaking as a witness here. He is speaking as an accused person standing in the dock as he is, and I regard where they are as the dock for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the procedure that I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So we could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It is, I think, the universal procedure in the jurisdictions that I've practised in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Delic can make whatever statements he thinks he could in mitigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to all. I am glad that after two years of being here I am finally able to address you. Initially, I did not want to speak, because I said everything I could to the Prosecution, but after the testimony of Esad Landzo, I cannot sleep at night because I never ordered Esad Landzo to kill anyone, to set anyone on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. This seems to be going to guilt or innocence at this point, instead of mitigation of punishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that anything that Mr. Delic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Supposing a person is convicted and the judge asks him what should be the quantum of sentence, can he, at that stage, say "I'm still innocent"?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It's confusing in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's not confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Can't he say that he was guilty or innocent?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Try to understand the ethics of the profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did think that this matter was going to proceed on the basis that it would only be matters in mitigation. I object if there is going to be any issues raised by the accused which go to the question of guilt or innocence, and I support my colleague in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that the rule that I'm familiar with is that anything this accused wishes to say that he believes could convince the sentencer to mitigate the punishment -- there's an absolute horror story out of a court in New York where a Mafia member knew he was going to get life, and he proceeded to curse at the court for an hour, and that was permissible. By the way, he did get life on that case. But whatever the defendant wishes to say is germane at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, let's not confuse the two situations where one is still pleading innocence. As I said from the beginning when we started, we've started a procedure which has some ambiguities in it. The accused persons are still under our Rules and our law and are presumed to be innocent. They are still, at the same time, expected to plead in mitigation of guilt. This is a fairly clear thing. But here, if the accused person wants to say anything which he expects the Trial Chamber to take seriously, he should not reopen matters which affect guilt. He should, as much as he can, plead, in explanation, of whatever might have gone against him and not say things which would appear to involve other accused persons at the trial. Because mitigation is mitigation as to one's own guilt and should not affect other persons in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think he wants to say anything that would affect the sentence that may be imposed if there's a finding of guilt as to any other defendant. That's clearly between the Trial Chamber and that defendant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Initially, I thought that when he opened with that statement, that it was just an opening statement, that he wouldn't go forward. I agree that if somebody says certain things against you, you might not sleep at night. That's understandable. But perhaps he might speak of matters in mitigation that are not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, since I didn't write this, and this is Mr. Delic's statement, I'm not sure what's going to be said next. I think if we just let him continue --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I just might make a suggestion, if he does go into matters of guilt or innocence, then he should be sworn and take the stand. If he sticks with mitigation of punishment, then he can have his unsworn statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Of course, I agree with Judge Jan, that a person who has been found guilty by a jury, he can then get up in front of the sentencing judge and say, "Judge, the jury has found me guilty, but I'm innocent, and please give me probation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think he is free to say whatever position he wants to and to make his plea in mitigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I agree with you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's hear Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. There's something wrong with our headsets. We're getting the wrong translation. I don't know what it is, but I can't follow the proceeding. I'm getting a different translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, the problem is that Mr. Delic's microphone is on, and it can be heard through his earphones. That is all it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Actually, I'm hearing two versions, the English version and the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I proceed where I left off?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, never in my life, while I stayed in Celebici, did I order Mr. Landzo. I'm looking at him in the eyes. I never told you to murder someone, to perform fellatio. Why aren't you ashamed of yourself to say that somebody told you to do so? You can lie to some people for awhile, but you will not be able to lie all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr. Delic is addressing Mr. Landzo. He is not addressing the Court right now, and he is still going to issues of guilt or innocence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, if you had this much in the approach to the matter, you could have also had Mr. Landzo go into the witness box and deny it, because this is directly alleged to him. This is not right. If you are making any statements in mitigation, the Trial Chamber will listen to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DELIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I could not even dream that somebody would be so rotten to tell somebody -- to be told, ordered, that somebody should be set on fire. I, for the first time, heard about the fellatio of the Djordjic brothers. I had never heard of it before in my life. I would only like to request one more thing. I have spent enough time, and I would not like to go to prison because of Esad Landzo's lies. This is all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There is nothing going to mitigation in this. It is not part of any mitigating evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on the fact that it was mostly addressed to Mr. Landzo and not the Trial Chamber and dealt with no issues concerning mitigation, I move that the whole statement, the whole right of allocation, be struck from the record and disregarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The Prosecution supports that application, Your Honour. None of it went to the issue of mitigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's not for you to say. The Trial Chamber knows what to take into account in determining mitigation or not. We've heard him, and it doesn't matter whether you made such a submission or not. We know what he said in his statement in mitigation. Mr. Moran, I think that's all we have from your --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Two little housekeeping matters. The registry has informed me that, one, they had to renumber those documents that I provided earlier today, and, two, I apparently forgot to move to introduce them. So with that, I would move to introduce those documents under whatever the proper numbers are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Whatever they are, you can move to introduce them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Again, just so the record is clear, for about the third time, we will be supplementing with the written statement, under whatever the next number is, for Mrs. Delic. With that, we rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Who is next?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Please, Your Honour, it now falls upon Mr. Mucic to present his submissions in mitigation. There are a total of six witnesses to give short oral evidence. My application, at this stage, is to adjourn his submissions until tomorrow, really, for two reasons. First of all, it's very late in the Trial Chamber's day, and the Trial Chamber has already heard a lot of evidence today. Secondly and pertinently, those witnesses were seen by myself and Madam Residovic until approximately midnight last night to get -- I beg your pardon, Madam Buturovic, perhaps an indication of how tired I am -- until after midnight last night to take proofs of evidence from them. The witnesses I know were, therefore, up until at least midnight, and they came to court this morning in anticipation of giving that testimony much earlier. I don't criticise my learned friend, Mr. Moran, but we all thought that the Professor was going to be, perhaps, an hour this morning and that they would be started --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's what we thought too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: The net effect is that the six witnesses have literally been sitting in a room all day now, and I don't think it would be fair to them or, indeed, to anybody else to expect them to give us their best at this time of day. As we only have something in the order of 14 minutes left, I make the application for an adjournment until tomorrow. I can give this assurance, that subject to cross-examination, we will go no further than lunch time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that's satisfactory to me, and I think my colleagues also agree. We can adjourn now and come back at 10.00 a.m. Yes, have you anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to ask the Court's permission to be excused from the proceedings for the rest of the week. Ms. Nancy Boler will be here to represent Mr. Landzo, but I would like to ask to be excused for the rest of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can be excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: 5.17 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 14th day of October, 1998 at 10.00 a.m.
